speechtext:

That this House commend the organizers of the petition for their continuing efforts to seek legislation to protect the unborn and thus foster a life-sustaining society.

That the government be instructed to cancel its proposed intention to make this change in the Unemployment Insurance Act.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR MORE FUNDS FOR MEDICAL RESEARCH COUNCIL-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
REQUEST FOR MORE FUNDS FOR MEDICAL RESEARCH COUNCIL-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I request the unanimous consent of the House to present a motion dealing with a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Considering that according to a study published by the Science Council of Canada, the National Research Council of Canada should normally have a budget of some $19.9 million to be able to bring their financing at the same level as in 1969, whereas for the current year, namely 1975-76, the budget of the council has been frozen at $10.9 million; considering that the Canadian Cerebral Palsy Association protest violently against the reduction of funds alloted to medical research and that they go as far as saying that these reductions are deplorable, and considering that in the budget of May 25, the Canadian government does not give priority to medical research, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier):
That this House order the federal government to take immediately all concrete measures required to enable the Medical Research Council to proceed with their works safely, and to face present and future health problems.

SUGGESTED DENIAL OF FARE INCREASE PENDING INVESTIGATION OF OPERATIONS BY AUDITOR GENERAL- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Yesterday the president of Air Canada announced that Air Canada will be seeking increased air fares in the near future. These proposed increases come within months of the previous increases of April 18. In light of the fact that fare increases are usually directly related to higher operational costs, and in light of the financial fiasco in the finance branch of Air Canada in Winnipeg, I would like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Whiteway):
That this House direct the Canadian Transport Commission to not consider any air fare increases for Air Canada until the Auditor General, under direction from this House, has had the opportunity to do a complete investigation of Air Canada's financial operations to determine that proposed air fare increases are justified, and furthermore that upon receipt of the Auditor General's report the CTC be informed as to whether or not such fare increases are justified.
Furthermore in light of the fact that Air Canada has not been before the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications since 1973,

that the president of Air Canada, Mr. Claude Taylor, be directed to appear before the Standing Committe on Transport and Communications immediately.

subsubtopic: PROGRAMS FOR THE ATLANTIC REGION-CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. It relates to the very strong statement issued yesterday afternoon by the Council of Maritime Premiers, in effect a denunciation of federal transport policy and raising specific questions about the co-ordination of such a policy with the government's program and the announced commitment to regional economic development. In view of the specific request by the Atlantic premiers made in February concerning the revised intra-regional freight assistance program and the fact that there has yet been no official response from the Minister of Transport, can he explain the shocking disregard of this request and what in fact is the basic commitment of the federal government in respect of the rationalization of the transport policy with other programs of economic development in the region?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS FOR THE ATLANTIC REGION-CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES
speechtext: Rather than a shocking disregard there was indeed careful consideration of the position, including a possible position which had been generally agreed upon between the Atlantic transportation ministers and ourselves with regard to certain freight subsidies, and on that further consideration we decided to have rather longer term discussions before making any move. Indeed, for the present time, therefore, there has not been any further action taken on the $5 million cut in the inter subsidy which had been proposed earlier. The discussions indeed will proceed, but any such action will only be taken when we are satisfied that what we are doing with the available money for transportation is in the best interests of the Atlantic provinces.

subsubtopic: PROGRAMS FOR THE ATLANTIC REGION-CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
I wonder whether the minister can indicate why no information was conveyed or no official response was given to the governments of the Atlantic provinces. In addition, can he indicate what steps have been taken with regard to the announced increase by CN and CP concerning freight rates as of July 1 for that region, and has the minister arranged any meeting with the provincial premiers in order to alleviate the obvious concern and anxiety they have with respect to federal transport policy?

May 27, 1976

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS FOR THE ATLANTIC REGION-CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES
speechtext: There are possible contacts at different levels, and the ones that I had foreseen were preliminary discussions between our officials and the officials from the Atlantic region. Indeed, I will be very surprised if those discussions have not already been under way. It may be that the premiers were simply not aware of what may be done. I obviously would be prepared to meet the premiers. I have a regular system of meeting with the Atlantic transport ministers, and I had thought that would be the ordinary way of going about dealing with transportation issues, but it does seem that each time the premiers meet they raise the subject in a significant way. I will certainly be delighted to join them at some meeting if that is their wish.

subsubtopic: PROGRAMS FOR THE ATLANTIC REGION-CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES
speechtext: In view of the fact that the council of premiers did issue this very strong statement, and considering their particular anxiety with respect, perhaps, to a decline in the federal commitment with respect to a co-ordination of transport policy in terms of the commitment to alleviate regional economic disparities, I wonder if the minister will indicate whether he stands by the same commitments made by his predecessor, now the Minister of the Environment, with respect to the fact that transportation policy had to take into account the special needs which exist in the various regions of this country, and if so, perhaps he would be prepared to make a statement shortly on motions with a view to alleviating the anxieties which presently exist in the region.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: PROGRAMS FOR THE ATLANTIC REGION-CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
There is certainly no need for the anxiety, and let that be the statement. In fact, the ongoing position is very much to take regional problems into consideration, and it is our intention-and I convyed this to the Atlantic ministers at our last meeting-to include that as a statement of principle in legislation which will be before this House in the next session, which is also known to them as being in our schedule.
Therefore, there has been every assurance. We have a regular and ongoing system of meetings with the federal and Atlantic provincial transportation ministers which can take all these matters into consideration. Indeed, we have ongoing and regular meetings of officials, and I think the system is working very well. I am somewhat surprised that there might be a breakdown in communication between the transportation ministers and the premiers of the Atlantic provinces.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister says that nothing is being done without consultation, and indeed, approval of the provincial leaders in the Atlantic provinces. Is he suggesting that the premiers or the appropriate ministers in the Atlantic provinces approve of the fact that of the $41.2 million removed from the transport budget as of December, 1975, some $22 million touched on the Atlantic region, and that the leaders in those provinces approved the provision in the bill before the House to delete the subsidy on the export of wheat and flour?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: POSITION OF ATLANTIC PREMIERS ON BUDGET REDUCTION AND DELETION OF SUBSIDY ON EXPORTED WHEAT AND FLOUR-CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make it quite clear that I did not say that in every case before action is taken there will indeed be approval of the region. That may be a bit too much to ask, in terms of the obvious desire on the part of any particular region not to pay additional amounts and to have increased and never decreased subsidies. Region by region that is understandable, but not very consistent with the over-all problem of spending in this country.
Furthermore, I would say that the figure is quite wrong in terms of the proportion of savings, and we discussed this fully with the Atlantic transportation ministers some months ago. Furthermore, wrong as it is, it includes, for instance, the very $5 million which, as I just indicated to the hon. member for Egmont, has not been gone ahead with even though the particular slicing of that $5 million was an agreed matter in terms of better re-arrangement of subsidies. Obviously, in regard to increases in ferry charges, those who have to pay them prefer not to pay them, but on occasion we have to face the fact that as costs increase, some charges have to increase too.

subtopic: POSITION OF ATLANTIC PREMIERS ON BUDGET REDUCTION AND DELETION OF SUBSIDY ON EXPORTED WHEAT AND FLOUR-CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES
speechtext: I take it that the minister approves of selective consultation. I would like to ask him whether he has had adequate consultation to work out an integrated approach to transportation problems in the Atlantic provinces with a view to fostering the development of those provinces rather than what seems to be a hit and miss effort on the part of his department to cut back on subsidies here and there.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: POSITION OF ATLANTIC PREMIERS ON BUDGET REDUCTION AND DELETION OF SUBSIDY ON EXPORTED WHEAT AND FLOUR-CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Halifax suggests that I have been talking about a selective approach but I have not. I have been talking about an all-embracing approach to consultation. If he thinks that what I mean by consultation is to give the final decision and an ultimate veto to a region, that is wrong. There is a need for the federal government to take some decisions and to take the responsibility for them. There cannot be a simple veto and control by any region in this country. I can assure the hon. member that there is the fullest consultation and consideration of the Atlantic need and the very organization of the committee of Atlantic transportation ministers with myself and with our officials working on an on-going basis is designed exactly for that purpose and will be doing a good job of it.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct my question to the Minister of State responsible for fisheries? subtopic: PROPOSAL TO GRANT EXPORT LICENCE TO SELL FISH OUTSIDE CORPORATION-REQUEST FOR ANALYSIS OF PROCESSING COSTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for giving me notice. In reply to his question I say that I remain convinced that the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation is the best vehicle for serving the over-all needs of fishermen through its single marketing desk approach. I am not able to agree with the hon. member's request, because I feel it would lead to erosion of the corporation and loss in the strength of the single selling desk approach, as created by the Act.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO GRANT EXPORT LICENCE TO SELL FISH OUTSIDE CORPORATION-REQUEST FOR ANALYSIS OF PROCESSING COSTS
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. As prices quoted at Motley, Minnesota, are 50 per cent higher than prices offered by the corporation and as the original concept of the corporation, that of a single desk marketing agency, is now saddled with an astronomically high capital cost, will the minister reassess his position and direct the corporation to open its books and analyse, per pound per species, the cost of the processing done by the corporation?

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO GRANT EXPORT LICENCE TO SELL FISH OUTSIDE CORPORATION-REQUEST FOR ANALYSIS OF PROCESSING COSTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member will recognize that it is not my function to direct a corporation of this type on a day to day basis. There is a board on which all provinces are represented. They are involved in the setting of initial prices which, recognizing the high costs of processing, are set as high as possible with the final price set at the end of the season. Because of a passing difference in prices, which might be very temporary, I am not sure whether the hon. member would like to erode the role of corporation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The House will recall that yesterday I had occasion to question remarks of the hon. member for St. John's East. He had characterized a recently concluded arrangement with the U.S.S.R. which will enable ground-fish plants in his riding and elsewhere to keep operating longer than anticipated, and which entails no trade-off from Canadian quotas as the "biggest sell-out ever". I took exception to this. Later I reminded the House that when we temporarily closed Atlantic coast ports to Soviet fishing vessels, the hon. member for St. John's East opposed this measure. The hon. member rose on a question of privilege denying this, and in response I agreed to check the matter out and report back to the House. I am now prepared to do so.
In Hansard of June 9, 1975, as recorded on page 6548, the hon. member made reference to the possibility of port closure as a "veiled threat which will have little or no effect on ICNAF nations", and also referred to the fact that "some of our ports .. .would be very seriously hit if they were closed". I must add, however, that later, in fact on the day I announced the closure as reported on July 23, 1975, at page 7854 of Hansard, the hon. member, in referring to this announcement, indicated that "we have all had to revise our thinking". speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am a little at a loss because I had hoped to have some further discussion with the House leader of the official opposition on the business. I have been having some discussions with him about the possibility of extending the hours of sitting to be devoted to the consideration of Bill C-84, and only for that purpose. There has been very great participation by members. I think it had been the hope of all members of the House that there should be an opportunity for as many members as possible

to participate in the debate. Therefore, in order to be able to complete our work by June 30, it seemed to us that the House should agree to sit some extra hours during the week.
I made some proposals which have been accepted by some parties but not yet by the official opposition. I hope that party will accept the proposals I have put forward. I have put them forward in a completely non-partisan way. They are perfectly reasonable proposals. We are discussing a bill which is not a government bill in the sense that there is any confidence attached to it. It is a bill in respect of which many members of the House wish to say something. There have been 65 members who have spoken already. I understand there are many more from the official opposition. I should like to see them have an opportunity, and I should like to see all of us get out of this House on June 30 with our business completed.
Another problem that has arisen is that I have had some preliminary discussion with the House leader of the official opposition about the possibility of dealing very quickly tomorrow with two bills from the Senate. I leave that open as a possibility. Other than that, we will continue with Bill C-84 on government days. There of course will be an opposition day on June 1, and the budget debate will be resumed on Wednesday. That will fill the rest of the week.
