subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are no fresh ideas in this budget. There is no new perspective, long range or otherwise, that would give Canadians renewed hope in our future, that would give them hope that our jobless will find employment, hope that our real
The Budget-Mr. Stevens
growth will regain what we lost in those sad years of 1974 and 1975, hope that we will regain our position in per capita national wealth among the nations of the world, hope that our $5 billion trade deficit will be lessened or eliminated. Confidence has been lost in Canada. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) did not help restore it in his presentation on Tuesday night. As one commentor has said, the message seemed to be: Economy, heal thyself.
Judging from responses to questions yesterday, the minister appears to seek his answers in the United States. He hopes their upturn will spill over into Canada without himself having to lift even a finger. The American motto is, as we know, "In God we trust". This administration's motto seems to be, "In the United States we trust". Meanwhile, this administration continues its spending spree. On Tuesday evening I pointed out that they has caused federal spending to quadruple since they took power in April of 1968. Expressed another way, in the nine years since gaining control of Canada, they will have spent twice as much as all previous administrations combined, that is, over the previous 100 years of confederation. On Tuesday we referred to the staggering deficits of this administration which will now total, in the aggregate, by the end of this year, $11 billion-an amount four times the size of all the deficits incurred, in aggregate, by the Pearson administration, the Diefenbaker administration and the St. Laurent administration.
Coupled with this high spending we must note that it is the average taxpayer in Canada who increasingly has been paying the shot. This year alone, aggregate personal income taxes will jump 26 per cent over last year. In 1968, the year this man Trudeau took power-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-personal income taxes represented 34 per cent of the total revenue received by Ottawa, while corporate taxation represented 15 per cent. Today, personal income taxes supply an amazing 53 per cent of Ottawa's take, while the corporate sector still accounts for that 15 per cent. In short, it is not the so-called fat-cat, it is not the wealthy, it is not that vague corporate entity which pays- in the main, it is the average, hard working Canadian who increasingly pays for the spending programs of this administration. In fact, taxation has gone so wild in this country that we now find the government is reverting to shell games in order to raise revenues still further.
Consider the approach of the administration to lotteries which it has aided and abetted with a view to increasing revenue and their take from Canadian citizens. Lotteries went out of fashion in the seventeenth century, and yet here we have a government in this century cultivating and developing that concept of raising money from the public.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Like Wintario.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Let us consider what this administration did with regard to the $100 Canadian gold coin. Yes, the administration is proposing to issue a $100 gold coin for $105, containing $32-worth of gold. That is what I mean by the shell game this government has become party to in order to continue raising money.

May 27, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Stevens
Let there be no mistake about it, in my remarks today I would like to indicate where at least $1 billion can be cut from federal government spending plans and where $500 million of that amount can be given back to the Canadian public, where it belongs, and something in excess of $500 million can be used to lower the $4.5 billion cash deficit proposed to be incurred by this administration in the current year. But let me first deal with the administration's wage and price controls. It now appears that this program was introduced at the wrong time, in the wrong way, for the wrong purpose and for the wrong length of time.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And with your support.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The controls program would have made sense 18 months earlier, but not during the current period when inflation is on the decline around the world, when we hover on the brink of recession, with 750,000 people out of work and when we have a need for more productivity in this country. Any controls program should commence with an absolute freeze for, say, 90 days, with a tempering of controls to suit the circumstances for another 15 to 18 months at the outside.
Hon. members will recall that this administration started with a consensus dialogue. That dialogue alarmed everyone. Then the government went into gentle controls, which were understood by few; and now, partly as reflected in the budget of last Tuesday, the government seems to be moving into extensive controls which will be policed by an ever-growing bureaucracy. Throughout the piece there has been a lack of meaningful dialogue with labour, with business, with the provinces and with the consumer in Canada.
When we clear away the sophistry surrounding this administration, it is more and more apparent that its interest in controls is threefold. First, this government believes it is popular, politically, to appear to be doing something to counter inflation. Second, controls give the government an opportunity to continue its spending habits in the mistaken belief that the wage and price control program will keep the lid on inflation which will ensue from its big spending and high deficits. Cut the minister's figures whatever way you like; the truth is that this government has allowed spending to increase by over 26 per cent per year for the last four years. With such a ravenous appetite for spending, no controls program will ever work.
Third, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) believes there should be greater intervention by government in our economy on a permanent basis. The recently announced northern land regulations perhaps highlight this type of thinking. The administration's refusal to outline options which will be open to Canadians in the post-control period confirms the belief that our control period is here for a long time, and chairman Pepin of the Anti-Inflation Board certainly leaves no doubt that he sees controls for an indefinite period in Canada. To suggest that the program should continue until December 31, 1978, or even longer, is alarming and particularly unfortunate. This administration should give a firm commitment today that these controls will not continue beyond another year. Twice the Liberal caucus, dominated by this government, defeated
[Mr. Stevens.)
our amending motions to terminate controls legislation by next April or May.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why wait for a year, if it is wrong now?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The members of the Liberal caucus are forgetting that the main reason Canadians have supported controls to date is that they believe they are temporary, and that is one reason we voted against this measure twice in this House, on the basis of it running longer than for an 18-month period.
History demonstrates the administration is wrong in its approach. Robert Schuettinger, lecturer in economics at Yale University, in an interesting survey of wage and price controls for 50 centuries, states, "For the past 46 centuries at least, governments all over the world have periodically tried to fix wages and prices. When their efforts failed, as they usually did, governments then put the blame on the wickedness of their subjects."
Already this administration cites the businessman, the labouring man, or the individual as the villain in our inflationary condition. It chooses to ignore that our inflation is due primarily to excess federal spending and, until recently, undue growth in our money supply.
Surely we can learn from history. Great Britain, over the past 30 years, followed a path surprisingly similar to this administration's economic approach. Now, as we see that country crushed economically and humiliated in the eyes of the world, can we not accept that serious mistakes were made? Why repeat the mistakes? The British approach to wage and price controls developed from attitudes that arose during the Second World War. In an article on wage and price controls entitled "The Lessons from Britain", Michael Parkin from the University of Western Ontario concludes, "The existence of controls has certainly contributed to Britain's last 25 years of slide into economic and social chaos." The message is clear. Let's heed it.
In the March-April edition of the Canadian Tax Journal, Professor J. B. Jump and Professor T. A. Wilson of the University of Toronto reviewed Canada's fiscal policy and ended with a damning indictment of the administration controls program. In their article they state:
With negative effects on investment spending and spending for research and development, the controls program will hamper productivity growth thereby reducing Canada's potential rate of growth and contributing to higher unit labour costs in the longer run.
We therefore cannot escape the conclusion that the present program should be either modified substantially or abandoned completely. To continue our present course will reduce the rate of growth of the Canadian economy in the near term by reducing real aggregate demand and in the longer term by reducing productivity growth.
What more need be said, Mr. Speaker, especially when we bear in mind that Messr. Jump and Wilson are advisers to the Department of Finance.
Now let me deal with agriculture. No other field or industry in Canada was so ignored in this budget as was the farming community. Despite the fact that it was the farmer who, through the sale of his goods, helped, lessen our trade deficit, the same farmer was virtually ignored in the minister's presentation. In our view, the farm community in Canada could, with proper federal direction and
May 27, 1976

incentives, be one of the most effective forces in increasing our export trade and thus reducing our trade deficits. Surely the Minister of Finance, who complains that world markets for our products are not available-we heard him say that here yesterday; that was the statement he kept making in this House, that world markets are not available for our products-would have to admit there is a market for food around the world. That market could be tapped more effectively, with better direction from the federal government. It is too bad the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) does not have the clout in cabinet to sell this concept.
Our farmers could increase production if they were given the opportunity. What finer way to reduce our trade deficit than to help feed more of the world's population? Let us take wheat as an example. We are a great wheat-producing nation, but I would suggest that we could be greater. How many people realize that France produces just about as much wheat as we do in Canada, or that India produces about one-third more than we do? How many realize that our production of wheat, expressed in tonnage terms, has been relatively static for ten years, while American production has jumped a dramatic 66 per cent? Incidentally, the Americans have sold much of that increase to foreign markets-the very markets the Minister of Finance says do not exist.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: At a loss!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I believe if the present administration would go to our farming community and say, "Start producing more, and we will start selling more of your goods in foreign markets," the product would be forthcoming and sales could be made. On agricultural products alone, the Americans turned from a trade deficit of approximately $5 billion to a substantial surplus within two years. They are still in surplus, while we nurse our $5 billion deficit. Mr. Speaker, I say to the minister: Let us start selling in markets that are there. In supplying those markets, let us make sure that the family farm is preserved. There is no reason why easier roll-over provisions for farms held within families cannot be facilitated, as several farm groups have requested. The family farm is an efficient unit of production and it should be encouraged to continue.
I should like now to touch briefly on the question of energy. At this point I would suggest that the energy price increases which have been announced are vital to federal finances. Without such increases, federal cash requirements would have mounted sharply and would probably have precipitated substantial changes in existing revenue and expenditure plans. I would hope that this new source of revenue would not be retained by the federal administration long after its initial purpose has been fulfilled. That initial purpose was to even out energy price costs in this country.
I think we must remember that the ten-cent tax on each gallon of gasoline which was imposed by this administration equals $3.50 per barrel for the oil itself. That is regressive, and I would point out that when the administration speaks about a $1.05 increase at the present time, with a further increase next January of 70 cents, it should be made clear that with their ten-cent levy alone they are extracting twice the per barrel amount from the Canadian
The Budget-Mr. Stevens
public that that increase is going to entail when it is fully felt by the public.
In fact, let the administration make it clear that it is not only a ten-cent excise tax they are taking; they are also taking a 3.9-cent sales tax from the Canadian public, or a total of 13.9 cents per gallon of gasoline. Put in perspective, the dealer who pumps the gasoline into the car gets 7.9 cents, on average, while the government gets 13.9 cents on the same gallon. That is why we say it is important that in future this ravenous government should not attempt to retain that source of revenue long after the need for it has gone.
I should like now to touch on the question of capital formation to look after future productivity needs and development in this country. There is nothing in this budget that will ensure there will be sufficient capital formation in Canada to fill our investment needs in the coming decade. It has been estimated that the gap between domestic investment needs and our domestic savings forecast could be as much as 10 per cent. Over the next decade, the cumulative shortfall could be as much as $75 billion.
We have three alternatives, Mr. Speaker. We could let our capital investment lag, which would mean less real wealth for Canadians and fewer jobs, or we could import savings from abroad, with the necessity of paying interest on those foreign funds in subsequent years, which in turn would heighten our trade deficit. Last year alone, for example, we borrowed $4.7 billion in this category- encouraged, incidentally, by the June 23 budget. This year we will start paying $400 million on that debt alone, and in subsequent years like amounts will have to be covered. Our third alternative is to encourage more capital formation in the country. How many people realize that, historically, four-tenths of our capital formation is in the corporate sector in Canada, yet that is the sector this administration chooses to kick around, to overregulate and overcontrol, with the net result that it is hampered in producing the necessary capital that we need for future development.
Does the Minister of Finance believe that his new AntiInflation Board formula to control profits will encourage capital formation in Canada? Not only will it not encourage capital but it will lead to further inefficiencies and lack of productivity in our industries. That is exactly what we do not need if we hope to regain our competitive position in the world.
Let me now touch on the Unemployment Insurance Commission. The members of my party commend the Minister of Finance for moving in some of the directions we have long advocated regarding changes in the Unemployment Insurance Commission program. In particular, we think it makes very good sense to recombine Canada Manpower and the Unemployment Insurance Commission into one unit. Indeed, it is hard for many on my side of the House to imagine the kind of convoluted logic which led to their separation in the first place. The changes in eligibility requirements and length of time for benefit payments represent a small step in returning the fund to an insurance concept whereby premiums paid in might be balanced by benefits paid out. We support the principle that the

The Budget-Mr. Stevens
government should provide an income to those who need it in our society, but have a fundamental objection to labelling the program as an insurance program when in fact it is not an insurance program. We are intrigued by the minister's concerns about regional disparity. We share those concerns and look forward to the chance of studying what the minister has in mind.
Having said all that, I am still amazed that this administration has failed to grasp that when a few people have to work to support the many who do not work, significant strains are placed on people of our society. Anyone with vision should be able to see that it is in our long-term interest to move as quickly as possible toward higher levels of employment. Why does this administration continue to highlight unemployment insurance and say so little about stimulating the economy and providing more jobs in the private sector for more people? How can the government tolerate the vague idea that if the United States recovery continues, and we get all the lucky breaks, we shall then create 250,000 more jobs when, at the same time, last year there were 350,000 new entrants to the labour force and there are likely to be as many entrants this year? How can you gloss over the fact that the most optimistic forecasts still indicate to this House that the government is following a budgetary policy which may well add 50,000 more people to the unemployment rolls which are already at the highest level of the last 15 years? We need a change in employment policy much more than we need further tinkering with our unemployment policy. I suggest it is time this government got its priorities straight.
Let us now touch on government expenditures. In the Minister of Finance and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien)-I am sorry he is not present-we have two of the finest diddlers in the land. Take a look at the Post Office, for example. In the estimates now before the House we are told that the department needs $1,122 billion for the current year. That does not sound too bad when you look at the expenditures estimated in the blue book for the fiscal year 1976.
Last year the department is reported to have spent $981 million, which means it is asking for an increase of $141,312,000, or 14 per cent. But then you find this crafty pair, the Minister of Finance and the President of the Treasury Board, start to fiddle. When you look at page 11 of budget papers "B" you are surprised to find that Post Office expenditures for the fiscal year 1976 are only $901 million, or $80 million less than we were told when the blue book estimates were tabled. Based on these figures, we find the Post Office estimates in reality have gone up $221 million, or 25 per cent in one year. Surely the people of Canada are entitled to an explanation. Why have the books been apparently cooked to show an additional $80 million as being expended in the fiscal year 1976, which of course makes the current estimates look more acceptable?
It is our suggestion that as far as the Post Office is concerned, until they can show otherwise their 1976 spending of $901 million should be taken as a base, to be increased by 14 per cent, the percentage they asked for, which would give a total increase of $126 million instead of the contemplated $221 million. Removing this diddle in the accounts would effect a saving for the people of Canada of

$95 million. In total, a review of the blue book estimates compared to the budget papers "B", page 11, reveals that there has been a misrepresentation of departmental expenditures in 1976 totalling $218 million. If that money was not needed in 1976, there was absolutely no reason for its being used as padding to justify a new estimate in 1977 which includes that amount plus an increase of 14 per cent or 15 per cent. The bulk of that money should be eliminated from present spending plans and returned to the people of Canada through a tax credit, or the cash deficit should be lowered. We reckon that including the Post Office's $95 million there is $225 million which could be eliminated from the 1977 spending plans of this administration, if they were prepared to be honest about their accounts. The fact is there. Let us cut it out. The average Canadian taxpayer needs that money more than do the ledgers and computers of the Treasury Board. If it is to be retained, then let us have a proper explanation as to why it is needed.
Lest you think that the $225 million misrepresentation, or error, in the accounts is but a single example, let me tell you of two other cases where the present administration appears to have altered the figures to its own advantage. The Minister of Finance notes that expenditures in the 1975-76 fiscal period are going to be somewhat higher- about 2 per cent higher. For this second piece of skullduggery let me take you back to the President of the Treasury Board's publication in February, entitled "How your tax dollar is spent." At pages 7 and 8 of that publication you will note that the President of the Treasury Board states that in the fiscal year 1976 total expenditures were $36.5 billion, and that in 1977 they would go up to $42.15 billion-as he said, a mere 16 per cent increase. The minister, on page 8, points out that this 16 per cent increase is the same increase as the previous year's. Included in the $42.15 billion are loans, investments and advances of a nonbudgetary nature totalling $2.75 billion.
Then on Tuesday night in walks the Minister of Finance, with his apparently innocent statement that he and the President of the Treasury Board have been surprised to find that the fiscal year 1976 figures have actually gone over the Treasury Board's final figure-I emphasize, final figure-by $725 million, almost three-quarters of a billion dollars. This conveniently put the minister in the position of being able to say that instead of growth in 1976 being at 16 per cent and in fiscal 1977 at 16 per cent, the actual growth figure was 18 per cent in 1976 and a mere 14 per cent in fiscal 1977. What sophistry! What diddling! Remember, we had been told less than one month before that the anticipated growth rate in this country was to be 13 per cent. Now we are told that real growth is to be 14 per cent or 15 per cent. The government had diddled its percentage figures and said that growth will be at 14 per cent to keep apparent spending in line with growth in the economy.
A review of the accounts reveals how this was cooked up. Certain Crown corporations and related entities- some, incidentally, under the direct control of the Minister of Finance-took down, in the aggregate, $725 million in fiscal 1976 rather than in 1977. By having these amounts reflected before March 31, the 1976 accounts were made to look higher so that the 1977 figure would look lower, percentage-wise. Here is the rub. Despite the fact that this extra $725 million was reflected in the 1976 figures, there is no credit for it now in the 1977 figures. The 1977 figures
May 27, 1976

show no reduction at all from the $42.1 billion figure to which I referred. To be consistent, 1977 spending should have been reduced by the same amount that 1976 spending was inflated, or by $725 million. But that is not the way these twins think. They now have $725 million to play with in the 1976 figures, and another $725 million in the current year.
These greedy, ravenous administrators who have control of this country have chosen to clutch on to this money because they know it gives them a slush fund of almost three-quarters of a billion dollars which they can squander as they see fit without meaningful recourse to the parliament of this country or the Canadian people. However, that is only part of the story of how they are handling your finances and mine and everyone's tax dollars in Canada.
In another section of the minister's speech he mentioned that $300 million will not be included for federal nonbudgetary expenses as they have asked Canadian National Railways and the Export Development Corporation to go out and raise the money directly. Remember, it was W. A. C. Bennett of British Columbia who first carried out that scheme. He cleared the British Columbia debt by having provincial Crown corporations take it over and then proclaimed the provincial government debt-free.
We are now told by this administration that they are saving $300 million. The fact is the money still has to be borrowed, and the covenant and guarantee they are giving is the covenant and guarantee indirectly of the people of Canada. Properly reflected, this $300 million should be added to what we understood was the ultimate figure to be spent in 1977, that is, to the $42.1 billion I referred to, the figure which the President of the Treasury Board told us only last month was the sky, the uppermost figure for 1977. For these reasons, we are asking the two ministers to give us an explanation as to why they cannot save for the people of Canada $225 million, as I touched on earlier, but why at least another $410 million cannot be eliminated from the non-budgetary side of federal spending for 1977. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) claims he is innocent of the charge of excessive spending, but he appears to have blackened the figures to make himself white.
In addition to the savings I have indicated, we believe the administration should tell us why $250 million cannot be slashed from the consulting and related contracts reflected in current estimates. These are only part of the contracts this administration has grown accustomed to awarding to their friends. Based mainly on the Auditor General's recommendations, we believe the administration should tell us why administrative savings cannot be realized and the civil service stabilized with a cost saving totalling at least $90 million. In addition, a systematic amalgamation of departments or the phasing out of departmental operations which overlap with other federal departments or provincial counterparts can realize minimum savings of $50 million.
Do we really need 29 ministries in Canada, when the Americans can operate a country ten times our size with half that number? Does it really make sense to have ten departments operating in each of our provinces when in
The Budget-Mr. Stevens
many cases their activities overlap directly with counterpart departments in Ottawa? I understand that on occasion these departments become counterproductive-one arguing with the other as to what should be done, with the result that nothing is done. To this end, it might be wise for the government to commission a Glassco-type commission to review the spending habits of this administration with a view to suggesting where savings may be made. After all, when the Glassco commission study was done in 1962, total federal spending was $6.5 billion. Today it is, on the same basis used at the time of the Glassco commission study, over $34.9 billion, a figure five times that of 1962.
In total, I have outlined possible savings of $1,025 million this administration could consider. Now, here is how we would like to see those savings used. First, we would like to give a tax break of $250 million to the Canadians who have been paying the shot. Of this amount we would like to see a 10 per cent tax credit-that would be about $100 million-go to those earning $8,000 or less. The remaining $150 million should be given in credits scaled down appropriately for those earning between $8,000 and $16,000. We believe it is time to give the taxpayer such a break, for three very good reasons. The April Economic Review reveals, at page 56, that the real gross national product per employee in Canada has actually gone down by $200 since 1972. In 1975, the average employee, in real dollars, earned $11,645 compared to $11,848 in 1972. Surely it is wrong to deny a tax break to such employees who are being required ti restrain their wage increases. Second, we would point out to the administration that they have reaping a bonanza in personal income tax aggregate increases which this year alone are jumping 26 per cent, or $3.3 billion. An 8 per cent reduction of this increase would not be out of line. Third, and most importantly, as we have already indicated, the administration just does not need the money. By being more restrained and by being more frugal there is no doubt they could save this amount and turn it back to the people we and they are supposed to be serving.
We would like to earmark another $100 million of our spending cuts to give further incentives to the private sector to encourage it to increase its activities in the research and development field. In this connection, we should have a further explanation as to why the administration chose to end assistance to small business under the Industrial Research Development Incentives Act. Our incentive scheme would be adjusted regionally to provide the greatest incentive in areas of disparity. For instance, locations in the maritimes would earn a 70 per cent credit, but locations in, say, Toronto, would earn 25 per cent. This administration only gives lip service to productivity and improving our trade balance which is really an $8 billion deficit. I am pleased to see the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson) here. We should never forget that before we sold our non-renewable assets last year, the total trade deficit in this country was $8 billion. We covered that deficit by selling $2.9 billion of our nonrenewable resources. That left a deficit of $5.1 billion, and even the administration admits that $5.1 billion deficit. We covered by borrowing, in foreign lands, $4.7 billion and allowing our cash reserves to go down by another $400 million.
13900

May 27, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Stevens
But let us not forget the point. We had an $8 billion deficit before we started to sell our non-renewable resources, and I would say it is wrong to continue to pay for current extravagances in the form of trade deficits by selling off non-renewable resources that we shall run out of some day. Surely, from an accounting standpoint, we should show our accounts on the basis of the situation before we sold these resources and after we sold them, and the administration should attempt to ensure a continuing benefit to Canadians with respect to the moneys received fron the sale of those resources. I have in mind something like the heritage fund in Alberta in connection with the sale by that province of its non-renewable resources.
The minister spent the greater part of yesterday's question period claiming that we cannot sell goods in foreign markets if the markets are not there. I say to him, "The markets are there, if you have the goods to sell; but you cannot get goods to sell if you keep shortchanging research and development in the private sector." Look at the facts. For the past ten years the private sector has spent .3 per cent of our gross national product on research and development. There has been little encouragement from the administration to increase this figure. On the other hand, the Americans spend 1 per cent of their GNP on research and development, and Japan and Germany spend 1.4 per cent of theirs. With our competitors spending such amounts on technology and the development of new products, is it any wonder that private industry here finds it difficult to compete in world markets? The minister is simply out of touch when he says the markets are not there. The markets are there. The difficulty arises through the failure of the present administration to give leadership and guidance to Canadian industry and to help them capitalize on those markets. By increasing our exports in this field we would lower our trade deficit in the most meaningful way-by selling merchandize, not non-renewable resources.
Tightly linked with this approach we would like to see another $75 million of the savings to which we have referred spent in giving export sales support and incentives to industry, especially to small businessmen who would increase their share of international markets. Surely, if the government is willing to give billions of dollars by way of assistance to large corporations, mainly foreign-owned, in the form of export credits it could give some assistance to our smaller concerns who could compete in these world markets if offered the opportunity.
Another $25 million of the money we suggest the administration could save should go into medical research in the hope that, through research, cures and preventive procedures could be found for many diseases which afflict citizens in this country. It is totally inconsistent to spend billions of dollars in the field of health and welfare while at the same time shortchanging medical research. Is it not sensible to find cures or, better still, to prevent diseases, rather than spend hundreds of millions of dollars treating people who become afflicted?
Mr. Speaker, all businessmen, and small businessmen in particular, are being swamped with increasing requirements to file government forms. This trend must be reversed. We believe the administration should be willing

to pay small businessmen for filling in federal forms, possibly by providing them with a suitable tax allowance. Hopefully, action along these lines would drive home to the federal administration the degree to which they are leaning on business to supply them with information which, very often, is never used. If they had to pay in order to get these forms completed, they might decide they did not need the information after all; they might even drop some of these forms. What a pleasant relief that would be for more than one million small businessmen who find the filling out of forms for the federal government one of the most onerous tasks they have to live with, when they would much prefer to be out selling their products or engaged in increasing their production?
In addition, we would like to see an incentive given to small businessmen to encourage them to increase their sales. As their sales increased over a certain level they would become entitled to a tax credit or rebate on a formula basis. In total, this form of assistance to small business and the form fees would take up $50 million of the unnecessary federal spending to which we have called attention. All in all, we believe $500 million of the $1,025 million we have identified could be given back to the Canadian people in the form I have outlined. The balance should be used to reduce the cash needs of the administration from $4.5 billion to $3,975 million. Such a cash deficit reduction would help renew public confidence in the economic future of the country. It would demonstrate to the Canadian public that, rather than continue to live with deficits, an attempt was being made to reduce those deficits. Capital markets would respond positively to such a move, and this in turn would encourage lower interest rates.
One of the most disturbing aspects of the budget is its lack of perspective. There is no long-range theme, no indication of where the administration sees the country going beyond 1977. We believe there should be a two-year review undertaken in every budget presentation, and a five-year perspective offered. In the United States, to which the Minister of Finance looks for relief, two-year budgets are required by law and a five-year perspective is given in addition. In that country they are much more frank with their people than the present administration is with Canadians. They spell out where they believe the country is going, then let their citizens judge the success or failure of successive administrations in reaching the goals set. In Canada we are told our real growth will be about 5 per cent this year, but this is not even a guess as to the situation in succeeding years. In the United States the long-term projections show a 6 per cent average rate of real growth from 1975 through 1981. Furthermore, this rapid advance in output is accompanied by a slowing of the inflation rate from 6.5 per cent in 1975 to 4 per cent, and possibly even 2 per cent. They show unemployment as deciding dramatically, well below the projection the Minister of Finance is holding out for Canada.
Mr. Speaker, the measures announced last Tuesday are not worthy of a budget presentation. Most of the items could have been covered in other ways. We are faced with an inflation rate of 9.4 per cent this year. This ought to be significantly lower. We are faced with current unemployment of 7.4 per cent and the situation is expected to be worse toward the end of this year: the figures will prob-
May 27, 1976

ably be even higher next year. That rate must be made lower. The real rate of growth in the economy last year was only .2 per cent, and the prospect this year is 5 per cent. It should be at least 6 per cent in this current year. We have an admitted deficit in trade of $5 billion, which is really the $8 billion deficit to which I have referred. We have interest rates 3 per cent higher than those in the United States, a country with which we are attempting to compete. It is with that background, Mr. Speaker, that I move, seconded by the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner):
To delete all the words following "That this House", and insert: "regrets the lack of any government commitment to the long-term growth and job potential of the Canadian economy, its failure to realize that sound economic growth and job creation are essential to effective control of inflation, and its refusal to impose any real and honest restraint on its own spending to ease the tax burden on Canadians."

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I first deal with a point of order before commencing my remarks. I intend to move a subamendment before concluding, and I understand because of that I will have 40 minutes in which to make my remarks.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is my understanding that the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) will have 40 minutes in view of the fact he is moving a subamendment.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I would have required two days if I had intended to reply to the previous speaker, but I am going to forgo that particular luxury. Let me say something about the statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) on budget night, in respect of which he has been suggested as saying he would rather be unimaginative than foolhardy. The minister managed the impossible task of being both unimaginative and foolhardy; foolhardy in the sense that he neglected in the most shameful way to do anything about that great forgotten problem of the Liberal government, namely, unemployment.
In many ways this is a political budget, not that all budgets are not political to some extent in that they all contain some element of politics. I would be naive to assume that they were not; but I have never, in my years in the House, seen a budget that was so totally political and totally responsive to an effort to correct the damage the Minister of Finance thinks his Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) did by his speech on New Year's. The budget is totally oriented to assuaging the business community to the belief that the new society the Prime Minister was talking about is unreal. He was trying to say to the business community, "Don't worry about it. This is still 'Canada Incorporated', with business as usual, and I am introducing a budget which will demonstrate that to you."
If you want some evidence of that, Mr. Speaker, let us look at the concluding remarks of the Minister of Finance when introducing the budget. His last paragraph is couched in the best of Bay Street terminology. The paragraph which appears at page 34 of the budget speech is as follows:
The Budget-Mr. Saltsman
We see ourselves as partners and not as sole proprietors in this enterprise. It is well to remember that in our economy there is not only a recognized role for governments and their enterprises but also and a massive and crucial role for private firms, labour unions great diversity of other private institutions and associations. If government alone is held responsible for the performance of the economic system, then government will be driven increasingly into the regulation of the private sector, at the cost both of efficiency and of economic freedom. In general we all look to the private sector to deliver the right goods and services to the right place at the right time and the right price. Productivity growth results primarily from the actions of the private sector, not the policies of government. The private sector can expect government to provide a framework of law and economic policy in which it can best function. But government can expect the private sector to operate efficiently, competitively and with due regard to the interest of society within that framework.
Never, in all the budget speeches I have listened to, have I heard such a denial on the part of the government of its own responsibilities. The budget reflects that, in that it says-almost in its entirety-that the government is not going to do anything. In some ways one gets the picture from the budget of the Minister of Finance, in an old jalopy going down a steep hill, with his foot on the brakes and his hands off the steering wheel, hoping to heck that a street called "Main Street, U.S.A." has been cleared for him. That is about the extent of the management he is putting into this economy with this budget.
The Minister of Finance is, in effect, saying, "Don't pay any attention to the Prime Minister's musings. Private industry is going to run this country as it always has, and not the government of Canada." He says, "To demonstrate that to you, we have given you a non-budget that in fact is not going to interfere with the marketplace in any way or try to manage the economy in any significant way". In other words, from the minister's point of view, the government that is best is the government that governs least.
The budget is a confused and impotent document that seems to have been put together by a committee, not of economists but of theologians. It seems to be an act of faith rather than anything based on economic doctrine and thought; sort of an Episcopalian belief, with faith that the great United States will save us. That country is going to be the cavalry which comes over the hill to the rescue of the Canadian economy. There are a number of problems with that kind of concept. First of all, we do not need the United States to save us. The minister, in his speech, seemed to be saying that unless the United States society recovers there is not much point in the Canadian government doing anything at all. That is the most shameful statement made by any minister of finance of this country.
Let us examine that statement for a moment. Granted, there is always some truth to the suggestion that our economies are interlocked. Let us look, for instance, at the manufacturing sector where the bulk of employment in Canada exists in terms of initial employment which feeds the service industry and other sectors above it. We find that the output of the manufacturing industry is consumed by the Canadian economy to the extent of 75 per cent, rather than by any foreign economy. We do not export manufactured goods, we export raw materials, and that is not a job-creating industry.
An article appeared in this morning's Globe and Mail which is very revealing. I wish I had the kind of confidence the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) seems to have that the United States economy is going to
95568-46 Vi

May 27, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Saltsman
do better than ours. That hon. member holds up the United States as the guiding light for Canada. Things are bad enough in this country without that kind of guiding light. The heading of the article in the Globe and Mail is "Consumer confidence down sharply in U. S." Surveys being conducted in the United States indicate that the present recovery is mild, and a pretty shaky one. In addition to that, there is concern that before that recovery gets under way, inflation will start again. Monetary managers in the United States are starting to tighten up their monetary policies and increase interest rates there. If we are waiting for a United States recovery-and I hope that country recovers, as I hope every country in the world recovers we may be waiting for a long time in vain.
In other words, even if the American economy does recover, what guarantee is there that we will follow suit? The Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) has taken considerable pride in pointing out that our economies have not been going in lock-step, that while the Americans suffered a high level of unemployment and inflation, in Canada we were doing somewhat better on the whole than the Americans. He is now reversing his position and saying that we are in lock-step because we have to wait for them to improve. The evidence is that by pursuing different kinds of policies we can do things the United States cannot do.
What really saved us in this country from the severest kind of depression was the unemployment insurance legislation we had, the old age pension legislation and the family allowances legislation. This provided a cushion and a stimulus to consumer purchasing power. That was absent to the same extent in the United States, and therefore the severity of the depression did not hit us as much as it hit them. However, if we look at the problem in the United States and assume that there will be an automatic recovery in Canada as the American economy recovers, we find no basis for that assumption. First of all, the slack in the United States is very great. Even if they recover to some higher lever of activity, what will they buy from Canada? They will buy the same things.
For a long time they have been buying our raw materials, which does not provide the same range of employment opportunity. If they step up their purchase of raw materials, we will have the same situation except that it will be exaggerated because the effect of selling raw materials to the United States will be that the value of the Canadian dollar will increase and we will be sucking in the manufactured goods, which is happening now and creating further unemployment in Canada.
What I am saying is that prosperity in the United States does not necessarily mean prosperity in Canada. Prosperity in the United States may very well be followed by a depression in Canada. Yet the Minister of Finance pins his entire policy in this budget on the hope that the American economy will recover and that we will get dragged along with that kind of recovery. That is fine management of the economy; that is great government we are getting! We might as well be paying our taxes to congress as paying them in this country, if that is the kind of management that is taking place. A budget is supposed to be an instrument for managing the economy, and not an instrument of

prayer. The cabinet does not look like a church, nor should it.
Let me take another example of the kind of situation the minister hopes for which may not materialize. In Canada there has been a fair demand for automobiles. Despite that, because of the lack of demand in the United States, our production in Canada has been declining and the imbalance of trade between ourselves and the United States has been increasing. The total imbalance in automobile trade is now close to $2 billion. In other words, we are importing $2 billion more, in terms of automobiles and parts, than we are selling to the United States. The Canada-U.S. auto agreement, with its main safeguards, still does not provide adequate protection for guaranteed production in Canada. The decisions that are made in respect of that agreement are made at the head offices of the motor companies of the United States, and the decisions are not always economic decisions based on where are the best costs or opportunities. Often they are political decisions.
If the American recovery should take place, it is not necessarily the case that we will receive an increased share of that recovery unless the American recovery takes place at such a pace that it is overheated and there is a surplus which must be purchased from other countries. In other words, before we can really count on the United States helping us, the improvement would have to be of vast proportions-and there is no evidence that that will take place. That is what the Minister of Finance is waiting for.
Other countries have managed their own prosperity. It is not as though this is a universal thing. Countries like Sweden, through proper planning, have in fact avoided some of the worst effects of the recession. Other countries have accomplished the same thing. Germany has accomplished very worth-while objectives by having better management of its own economy. Therefore, it is important that this country not be complacent, that it not sit back, and that it not wait for a foreign recovery in order to get the 7.4 per cent unemployment rate down in Canada.
It is for that reason we have advocated there be tax cuts in the economy at the lower end of the scale. The budget in fact does contain some tax cuts, but they are at the upper end of the scale in terms of registered retirement savings plans. There should be tax cuts at the lower end of the scale, because this would do two things. It would encourage consumers in Canada to purchase goods, and it would also restore some element of fairness to a tax system which badly needs that fairness restored.
The government and the minister may argue that this would be inflationary. Yet there is evidence that it need not be inflationary. The Conference Board of Canada pointed out that government deficits are not the cause of inflation. Other people in the business community also pointed out this situation. Therefore, it is important that purchasing power be restored in the economy. Very often, tax cuts and planned deficits result in surpluses, because if you can get the economy going again and can notch up some of the unemployment that is taking place and stimulate the economy in that way, there are very substantial savings from not having to pay out as much in unemployment insurance and welfare payments as well as having tax collections from those who are working.
May 27, 1976

A tax cut would encourage investment as well. My friends to the right seem to argue there has to be direct encouragement to investment. The experience has been that investment takes place when there is purchasing power in society. If there are customers whose needs need to be satisfied, industry will invest. At any rate, there does not seem to be any great need for additional investment to get the economy going, since the manufacturing industry is operating at only 80 per cent capacity and we must vastly increase the output of our society if in fact there is purchasing power in our society.
There are many things we could do aside from increasing purchasing power. There could be more direct government expenditure in things like improvement of the railbeds in Canada, which would have a significantly important job-creation effect. This would provide work for people directly on the railroads. It would provide work indirectly in places like the Sydney steel mills where the rails could be made. The Canadian government is talking about reviving passenger service in Canada. If there are expenditures needed for that, what are they waiting for?
Surely now is the time to proceed with these matters, when we need the employment and stimulus in this country. Yet there does not seem to be any response from the government in that area. If I were the prime minister, I think I would be suing the Minister of Finance for alienation of affection.
I mentioned earlier about consenting adults. This is not adult, and this is not consent. I pointed out earlier in my remarks the great rhetoric in the Prime Minister's New Year's address, the talk of a new society and the forwardlooking adherence and devotion to the Galbraithian ideas. These have been shot down in this budget by the Minister of Finance. I do not see how the Prime Minister can ever again call himself a Galbraithian. In fact, he has betrayed the central ideas of Galbraith. It seems that that great vision has now gone out the window and that the Prime Minister is in bed with the Minister of Finance and his unimaginative ideas.
The whole point of the Galbraithian thesis-and I think it is important to deal with this-this was the idea that brought in the wage and price controls program of the present government-is that you bring in that kind of system in order to enable you to do good and intelligent things. The government brought in the control system with all that is wrong with a control system but without any compensating merits which would enable them to use the control system for good things.
If you look at what Galbraith had to say about what he would do once a control system was in, you find that the government is doing none of these things. Galbraith said that the first thing you do is to improve the progressiveness of the income tax system; you lower taxes for people at the lower end of the scale, and you increase them for people at the higher end of the scale. That is what a control system is supposed to help you do. The idea of the control system is to keep a lid on inflation in order to enable you to stimulate the economy and to achieve more fairness in the incomes of people. So you would want a progressive tax system. We do not have a progressive tax system, nor is
The Budget-Mr. Saltsman
there any indication that the Minister of Finance intends to have it. Rather than do that, he has improved the amount of money that can be set aside for the registered retirement savings plan. He lifted the amount that can be set aside to $5,500. In other words, you can save up to $5,500 of your income, put it in a registered plan, and pay no taxes on it at all. Who has $5,500 to save? Certainly not the ordinary people of this country. If we look at the experience of the registered retirement savings plan and at the experience of some of the other programs that the government has set up, we find that even though it does not look like a tax break for the upper income people, the effect of all these new programs has been to enrich those who already have money, to the disadvantage of those who do not.
Let us take a look at the indexing which the government has brought in. The effect of indexing on tax reduction is startling. By the government's own figures, a married taxpayer with two children who makes about $10,000 can expect to have his taxes reduced by about $150. In 1976, through indexing, a similar taxpayer in the $30,000 bracket will save about $470, while a similar taxpayer in the $50,000 range will save about $680. The 38.4 per cent of tax filers who reported under $5,000 income received the grand total of .2 per cent of the tax savings from the deductions listed; that is, 38.4 per cent of tax filers had an income under $5,000, yet out of every $10 that was saved in taxes because of these programs, this group got just 2 cents out of the $10. The 2.4 per cent of tax filers who reported incomes of over $25,000 managed to snag just over 35 per cent of the total tax savings to be had from these programs. Out of every 1,000 tax filers, it were in the $25,000-plus category, yet out of every $1,000 saved because of these gimmicks, this small group saved $350 million of it.
The benefits of half taxation on capital gains are also enormous and concentrated in this top group. The top 2.4 per cent had 52 per cent of the taxable capital gains in 1974. This amounts to tax savings of about $31 million in 1974, a gift from the government to the richest citizens of the country. At the other end of the scale, the effect of half taxation of capital gains was the tax savings of some $171,000 spread over some 4,400,000 tax filters. The top 2.4 per cent saved over $88 million in taxes in 1974 through the registered retirement savings plan and just under $150 million from the total of exemptions as I have listed them.
The bottom 89 per cent, everyone with $15,000 income or less, saved just under $40 million through the RRSP and about $138 million from the total of exemptions. So we have 2.4 per cent who saved $88 million through this plan, and 89 per cent who saved $138 million from this plan- hardly an equitable system and hardly the kind of thing that the Prime Minister's love affair with Galbraith would indicate would be the correct thing to do.
There is an interesting editorial in the Ottawa Journal of March 30 in which reference is made to some of the loopholes which exist in the registered retirement savings plan. It is headed "Loopholes to stroll through", like walking through the tulips. It reads:
Let nobody deny that Canada is a land'of opportunity. Just consider a few of the opportunities created for Canadians by the federal government:
They can borrow from the bank at 13 per cent, invest the money at 10 per cent and make $200 or so in profit every year at the expense of other

May 27, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Saltsman
taxpayers. They can set up a registered home ownership savings plan in order to buy back a share of the house they cleverly transferred to the wife or husband the year before. Or they can collect the same $5,000 or more in tax savings by buying furniture for the house they already owned.
They can get the government to subsidize a foreign vacation by establishing a few years' worth of tax-sheltered registered retirement savings plans, then taking a year off in order to cash in funds at a large tax saving-several thousand dollars' worth for those who can wait a few years for the holiday. They can accomplish a similar tax saving without quitting work or taking a holiday by setting up a few years' worth of retirement plans for a wife or husband and then having the funds cashed in during the year in which the spouse's other income would be low.
Few, if any, countries in the world can match these and other opportunities for taxpayers to get something for almost nothing without even needing an accountant to figure it out. Just reading the financial advice columns in the newspapers would provide all the basic guides to the loopholes.
There is another excellent opportunity that is provided in this new society. If you invest in Canadian corporations and you get an income of $15,000 from the investment, it is all tax-free. Compare that to the situation of the man who works in a shop and earns $15,000 a year, if he is lucky enough to earn that. He would pay a substantial amount of tax. But you can invest in corporations and get some tax-free income. The story in the Globe and Mail of Thursday, May 30, headed "Investing in Canadian corporations could mean tax-free income" tells you how to do it. That is part of what our complaint is. I will not read that story. The techniques for doing it are there, and there are many people who take advantage of them.
Galbraith, in case the Minister of Finance has forgotten, or in case the Prime Minister has not reminded him, wanted a more egalitarian income distribution. Where is that in the budget? This budget, in fact, takes some of the advantages which I have outlined which already exist for upper income people in the home ownership plans and the registered retirement plans and gives them additional benefits, and the same kind of income distribution will take place. Those who have a great deal of money will get the tax-free benefits, and those at the bottom who can barely make it will get nothing at all. They do not have $5,500 per year in clear savings to put into these registered plans, and therefore they do not get the benefit. Is that the more egalitarian income distribution the Prime Minister has seemed to be so taken with?
Galbraith pointed out that there is a need for more government spending when the economy is flat. He did not suggest to the Prime Minister or to those here in Canada who read his interviews that we should wait for the American economy to correct itself. He said that if the private sector is not producing and providing jobs, then it is a government responsibility to see that jobs are created to stimulate the economy. However, above everything else the central part of what he was saying was that there must be full employment in society and that no government has any excuse for not moving and bringing in policies which create full employment. Instead of the government moving to full employment-and it obviously has no intention of bringing in policies to bring about full employment but is only praying that something will happen south of the border-it is going to do something else.

If the government cannot bring about full employment, how about knocking all kinds of people off the unemployment insurance rolls? Therefore, the government is suggesting a series of moves which would ask the poor in many of the areas of Canada where there is not any employment to pay for their failures and giving them the kind of aura which has been suggested by my friends on the right that they should have. The government is trying to out-conservative the Conservatives in terms of the approach it is taking with regard to the Unemployment Insurance Act. I have been critical of the Unemployment Insurance Act, as have many people. We know there are abuses in the act, and all of us are interested in correcting the abuses; but why does the government not work on those abuses, rather than throwing people out of work off the rolls? The greatest abuser of the Unemployment Insurance Act is the government itself by tolerating this level of unemployment.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Any government which cannot produce employment is not worthy of that name, and because it has failed to provide the kinds of policies which will produce employment, and it is not prepared to intervene in the economy to see that there are jobs for people, it has no right to say to those who are collecting now that they are off the rolls. In many ways, the decision of the government to increase the qualifying period from eight weeks to twelve weeks is probably not going to have the results the government thinks it will. It will not really save the government the amount of money it expects. If it does, it will not be a total saving. It will be at the expense of the provincial and municipal governments which will have to pay out money to cover up what the federal government is not paying. In fact, it is going to be a forced transfer payment from the provincial and municipal governments to the federal government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Welfare!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
People will be thrown onto welfare. The other day, when I raised this question with the minister during question period, he became highly indignant and suddenly started to spout figures which a little while ago he claimed he did not have. He had no idea, and I do not think he knows now what the consequences will be. At the present time, even with the eight-week qualifying period there is a serious problem. Somebody who is between jobs, waiting to go back to work and is offered a job and takes it-a job lasting a week, two weeks or three weeks-will lose his unemployment insurance as a consequence. If that waiting period is increased from eight weeks to twelve weeks, how much less incentive will there be for people to take temporary jobs to get off unemployment insurance, to the extent it is possible, until they can get a full time job?
The minister and the government have no right to throw the burden on the unemployed in this country. This problem cannot be dealt with when there are no jobs available. When there are almost 800,000 people looking for jobs, and less than 60,000 jobs listed, how can we put those people to work? We cannot. How do we know who really wants to work, and who is abusing the system? There is no way of telling. Until the government moves to full employment
May 27, 1976

and has some kind of industrial strategy for grading employment, and until it stops waiting for the United States and comes up with some regional policies which make sense, it should not throw people onto welfare by removing them from the very thing which has saved us from a very serious recession.
Because of that, I want to move an amendment to the amendment. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the amendment be amended by changing the period at the end thereof to a semi-colon, and by adding immediately thereafter the following words: "this House regrets in particular that at a time when more than 760,000 Canadians are unemployed the government has announced its intention to change the minimum qualifying period for unemployment insurance benefits from eight to twelve weeks".

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always with a certain amount of anxiety that members and constituents alike look forward to the budget speech, because in any society and organization, finance and budget matters are always of paramount importance.
Before I get on with my remarks, I would quote some excirpts from an article that appeared in La Presse of May 26, 1976, that is a report on the currant ACDA conference in Vancouver, under the headings:
Six hundred million more units needed within the next 30 years.
The Budget-Mr. Rondeau
I find stated in that article:
Our cities and towns ... lack jobs, are chocked with pollution, overpopulated, crammed with slums, devoid of adequate transportation facilities and faced with a rising crime rate.
And further in the same paragraph:
There are not enough jobs and housing.
How is it that a foward-lacking society such as ours should run shot of jobs and housing?
The next paragraph quotes the following words by the Right Honourable Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), which were probably referred to at that conference. He said:
In the search for human dignity, housing is a vital need, along with food and health. However, no country in the world not even those with the most advanced technologies, not even those with the most temperate climates can boast of providing adequate shelter to all its citizens.
I agree with that statement. But Canada, a country with the most advanced technologies, could have acted just the same with the best financial technologies, if the will had been there to considered a leader. If we have housing technology and lack the financial technologies needed to meet the current and genuine needs of the people, our present problems will remain.
Mr. Speaker, this budget is no surprise for newspapermen nor members. In my view, it brings forth nothing new, nothing exciting. It is more or less the same old thing I have been hearing under six different Ministers of Finance.
It shows again the same financial thinking, it reveals another aspect of a new tax which Canadians will have to support. Mr. Speaker, unfortunately our economy is running too fast and yet the government economists do not seem to have other solutions to put forward to help the government, because I know very well that it is not the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) who develops the financial policy of Canada, I am not that credulous, yet it is the government economists who control the Minister of Finance and are responsible for what we see now.
I would like to say that in Weekend Magazine of April 24, 1976, page 5, a journalist rightjfully makes fun of economists. The headline of the article reads:

And if we examine the present financial policy of the government and the results it has given in Canada, we can say that this series of six different cartoons show, if I may say so, the outstanding features of our Canadian economists and where they are leading us. They are represented by four individuals-let us say, the Minister of Finance and three economists-on a boat, at sea.
In the first cartoon, we see those economists discussing economic problems among themselves while they are slowly sinking: the boat is taking water, there is a hole in it, and it is sinking gradually, just like our Canadian economy. All the while, our economists continue making grand plans, voicing grandiose theories. This is what one of them says:
... Depressions and recessions were part of the normal cycle of ...

May 27, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Rondeau
Depressions and recessions are part of normal cycle, indeed! The other one says:
... Solution to the problem is ...
But he does not say.
The boat continues sinking ever so slowly. In the second cartoon, one end of the boat has already sunk quite a way into the water. One economist declares:
... The nature and role of the free market system ...
And so they continue enunciating theories while sinking.
The other says this:
... That consists in defining scientific excellence as ...
He is already half submerged and he keeps on making theories.
In the third cartoon, the economist gives a new theory:
... By stimulating demand and production by manipulating the money supply ...
This is what they do indeed. We in the Social Credit Party know this very well.
There, we see the boat completely submerged and we see the heads of the four economists out of the water. Another economist says:
... Building economic model of .. .
The caption on the fourth cartoon reads:
... Once we abandon present theory of ...
The other economist says:
... Short-term analyses which guard against...
And there you see the head of one economist disappear in the water and the three others have only their heads showing. In the fifth cartoon, the economist says:
... Neo-classicism is a "microeconomic" theory that...
Then, under he goes. The last one says:
. .. Whatever the market will bear .. .
And the boat diseappears completely. The last cartoon in Weekend Magazine of April 24, 1976, page 5, shows only the sea. The boat has disappeared and so have the economists.
Tuesday night, on television, the Minister of Finance seemed to be already in water up to his waist, because he let himself be guided in the boat of finance by economists who have never brought anything else to Canada but deficits to maintain the financial system we have been denouncing for more than 30 years.
Mr. Speaker, it is absolutely ridiculous and unthinkable to see to what extent, from the mathematical and financial point of view, this country is going adrift and to find out again that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) is having fun in the same boat with the same economists who give him the headaches which we know he has. Now, what struck me first and other hon. members who attended the reading of the budget around six o'clock, before the Minister of Finance made his speech in the House, was that inflation is good for the federal government because, without even touching the tax scale, it takes just under $4 billion more from personal income.

Last year, personal income gave the federal government a total revenue of $12,703 billion without taxes being increased. Because of inflation and as a result of the government financial policy creating inflation, $16,040 billion will be paid by Canadians in 1976, without taxes being raised. This means that inflation now allows the federal government to pocket almost $3.5 billion, without higher taxes while corporate taxes will bring $120 million more in the coffers of the Minister of Finance, which represents a 2 per cent increase for companies.
Mr. Speaker, the last six ministers of finance have always sung the same tune, come up with the same refrains. They do not change their tune and keep telling the Canadian people: Tighten your belts, live within your means.
The budget before us shows a $5 billion deficit, which clearly indicates the federal government is living above its means. How can the people be expected to live within their means, just because they cannot involve everybody into debts to finance their expenses, and trust a government which preaches restraint while incurring a $5 billion deficit?
Mr. Speaker, during the financial year 1976-77, the federal government will spend some 28 per cent of the gross national product. And I have in my hand figures which show that when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was elected in 1968, the total yearly expenditures of the federal government amounted to $13.9 billion. Today, they reach $40 billion, that is a 300 per cent increase over six years. In 1963, those expenses represented $737 for each Canadian whereas today they amount to $2,600 for each Canadian or $7,860 a year for the average Canadian family. On page 21 of the French Maclean of February 1976, an accountant from Quebec City, Mr. Marcel Belanger, who has been for 15 years member of five inquiry commissions-two federal, three provincial, including one on taxation-and who is now president of the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants-as far as I know, he is not an idiot nor a social crediter-says the following:
Twenty five years ago, all governments ...
All governments, not only the federal government, but all governments-
... were spending about one quarter of personal and corporate income...
Today the federal government alone is spending 28 per cent-
That is it, 25 per cent of what we call the national product. Today, the figure is 40 per cent. In the United States, it is about 32 per cent.
Further down in the same article, he says:
. .. Taxation sooner or later generates inflation?
The government is trying to find the causes of inflation and Mr. Marcel Belanger, president of the Accountants Association of the Province of Quebec, who has chaired five royal commissions of inquiry, two of which under federal juridiction, says himself that taxation-and if anyone knows about taxation, an accountant does, since that is his job-generates inflation.
... And when taxation starts to generate inflation, you have a very strong indication that your relative limit has been reached.
... Therefore, the limit is not theoretical.
May 27, 1976

That is not theory, that is facts.
It becomes perceptible.
That is why I said: Stop! Call a moratorium on fiscal changes, on new programs, and try to cut back government expenditures. Or at least slow down their increase . ..
Mr. Speaker, these people also agree with the position we have always taken in this House that inflation results from financial pressures exerted on the provinces, on their taxation system by the federal budget. Quebec municipalities are faced with the following situation. Some of them are now increasing their property assesment for 1976 and 1977 by 1900 per cent compared to 1975.
Since the provincial government is forced to change its property assesment in the province of Quebec due to the financial pressures exerted by the fiscal and monetary policy of the federal government, a 15-acre piece of land in the suburbs of Quebec City assessed at $11,670 in 1975 was assessed at $224,700 in 1976. The owner will have to pay in property only, let alone school taxes, $3,292 compared to $435 in 1975. Another taxpayer in Sainte-Foy who paid $40 in 1963 on an assessment of $4,400, will pay $588 in 1975 on an assessment of $33,450.
Mr. Speaker, when we go back to 1940 and look at the federal budgets, we note that in 1975 corporations paid 75 per cent of all taxes and in 1976-77, the national budget will be kept afloat by companies and corporations at a rate of 17 per cent; in other words, while personal income tax has increased, the corporate tax has decreased. As compared with 75 per cent in 1940, today, 17 per cent of the federal budget is being paid by corporations.
Mr. Speaker, I will not waste any time dealing with unemployment insurance. However, personal income tax has increased and the taxpayers will still be paying in 1977 almost $3,500 billion more in personal income tax, although income tax rates have not increased. Unemployment benefits will be reduced by approximately one half; in the words, theoritically speaking, instead of receving unemployment insurance benefits for 52 weeks, because of the new rates which have just been tabled, the same unemployment people will receive benefits during 26 weeks.
Mr. Speaker, one has to change the resources in the system being advocated. When we realize that a federal government, through its financial and monetary policies, can change the resource situation of a province or of an individual, then we must do something. The federal government has not always listened to the advice given him by economists. They listen to the economists who are in their employ, but pay no attention to those outside the House. In Le Devoir of May 31, 1971, it was reported that an economist employed by the Royal Bank of Canada, Mr. Reuber, has stated the following:
Ottawa should reduce personal income tax and sales taxes.
Ottawa does exactly the contrary in its present budget.
The government should reduce personal income tax and sales taxes to encourage productivity and decrease wage inflation, said the economist Grant L. Reuber, Director of the Department of Economics at Western University in London.
According to Mr. Reuber, the Bank of Canada worsened the economic problems of Canada by going from one extreme to the other and alternating credit restrictions and capital inflow in the banking system.
The Budget-Mr. Rondeau
This economist is stating that it is not by reducing the money supply of a country that we lower interest rates. When we restrict the money supply of a country, we automatically boost interest rates and automatically fuel inflation in an economy. When will the federal government stop listening to the economists of the Department of Finance and believe the economists of other spheres of the Canadian economy who have other concepts than the endless deficits, increases, taxes and levies. This economist went on to say:
.. . Canadian taxes are traditionally high and compared to United States tax reductions, they could be the basis of radical changes in the tax system.
And I was referring to a speech. It was certainly not delivered by an idiot as the speaker was the Hon. G. V. Clyne, Chairman of the Board, Chief Executive Officer, McMillan & Bloedel Limited.
