He made that speech on April 29, 1969 and he predicted what is happening today. He is a businessman who can usually see beyond the end of his nose and who is well known by the economists. I quote: [English]
It has recently been said in NDP political circles-
And it could be applied to the Liberals to demonstrate the same thing.

-that the British Columbia forest industry is not paying sufficient tax and is not bearing its fair share of the cost of government. Let me give you some figures from our own company, so that you can judge the truth for yourselves. ... the profit of our Company was $38.8 million for 1968 .. .
We paid $36,500,000 in current income and logging taxes and set up a provision of $3,500,000 for deferred taxes, making a total liability of over $40,000,000 by way of income taxes. Then we paid another $20,000,000 odd to all levels of government by way of property taxes and fees, property rentals, federal and provincial sales taxes, stumpages, royalties and severance tax. In other words, in order to earn $38.8 million last year, this Company had to pay to governments at all levels $60.3 million.

Even before McMillan & Bloedel Limited could make a profit of $38.8 million, they had to pay $60.3 million in taxes to the government. Here is what he said:
(English]
In 1968, after allowing for interest expense, we made only 6.7 per cent on our net total assets. ... last Thursday the bids for treasury bills, and as you all know treasury bills are 90-day obligations of the government of Canada, ranged up to 6.78 per cent. ... Considering the risks, then, it cannot be said that 6.7 per cent is too great-
And this is what he said about Mr. Rasminsky who was then the Governor of the Bank of Canada.

-government costs are still rising and expenditures increase as government departments continue to seek out more and more areas of our national life in which they feel that they should intervene. Federal spending has risen from $7.7 billion for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1966 to $10.7 billion budgeted for the fiscal year ending March 31 of this year.
Mr. Speaker, that was in 1966-more than ten years ago. And this is what he said when comparing the Canadian and the U.S. tax system which the Minister of Finance

May 27, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Rondeau
likes to interpret as being comparable with that of our country.

A Canadian earning, say, $30,000 a year, married with two children and paying, say, $2,800 a year in interest and property taxes, would pay about $9,550 in income taxes in Canada ... In the United States, a man with a similar income would pay about $5,750. Now, what concerns me is this, that in that income bracket are men with the kind of talent which Canada badly needs-men with leadership qualities and capacity for innovation. When they are attracted to the United States by improved earning conditions there, Canada loses a resource more valuable than her trees and her minerals.
-the danger of increased taxation ... is a threat to our economy. Canada, with her great resources, faces a future which may bring great prosperity, or it may, by reason of poor government and ill-advised taxation policies, fall into a state of stagnation such as has been experienced from time to time in other countries.

Mr. Speaker, I could go on speaking all day to show that this taxation system, this fiscal system, this monetary system, on the one hand penalize the worker, and on the other, discourage businessmen except those who have learned to evade income tax by the means that I shall enumerate, except the big companies-and I cannot blame them-who take indirect means to evade taxes and manage not to give away all their profits.
I also have here an extremely interesting article which appeared on page 31 of the March 1976 issue of MacLean s and which was written by two highly qualified reporters, Jean Pare and Walter Stuart, about Tax Evaders, and I would like to quote a few very concrete examples:
With $100, you can set up a ghost company, and with $500, you are tax exempt for 30 years.
And I would like to go a little further and read a few extracts from this article in order to make my point.
In the Cayman Island Handbook, a tourist-oriented brochure, it is said:
Taxes are the scourge of the twentieth century, just like world wars, overpopulation and pollution.
Social Creditors for their part say "pollution through finance". I quote:
There are people who are victimized by overtaxation such as existed in the worst tyrannies of Ancient times ... It is quite natural that you should want to protect your property against thieves and income tax collectors!
I am quoting from the Grand Cayman tourist magazine.
It is estimated that there are 155,000 ghost companies that only serve to protect profits which should normally have been taxed. Last year, there was a travel agency selling a world tour of tax havens.
This means that tax havens were specially advertized.
-(there are more than 30)-
-in one island only.
-for the ridiculous sum of $1,750, which is deductible from taxable revenue in any case.!
-every dollar sent under the tropics by a large company or a rich spendthrift must be replaced with a dollar taken from the income of a worker, most often a poor one. The Gaspe fishermen, the Port-Cartier lumber workers, even the Olympic stadium plumbers are unable to hide their income from the tax collector: They are the ones who pay for "fiscal tourism".
The federal Department of Revenue is completely in the dark as to the amounts lost in this manner: "We do not even have enough information to give us an idea of the scope of the problem. Until now, we have

recovered $10 million, but this is only the tip of the iceberg. Some people are talking about $100 million a year, others of $1 billion!
... Even the most famous and the most pretentiously honest banks do chip in. There are 186 of them in Grand Cayman, that is one for every 63 people!
... Any individual may set up a Grand Cayman ...
-And I could quote, Mr. Speaker, a host of other countries where at present, through multinational companies, Swiss banks, banks in the Bahamas, in Panama or in Grand Cayman, companies may evade taxation and this is perhaps one of the reasons why we now see that companies-I will give other figures later on-are not increasing the federal tax intake. Because today they want to save their undertakings they use all legal means at their disposal. I do not say these companies are acting illegally, no they are acting legally. I continue this quotation:
.. . Any individual may set up in Grand Cayman a joint-stock company by paying $100 in incorporation fee and an annual contribution of $50. As long as this company's profits are coming from outside, Grand Cayman will not collect any taxes. They can even get a tax exemption for 30 years on paying a $500 permit!
Profits made in Canada by your "foreign" company and directed to Grand Cayman are tax free until you decide to get them back ... if someone happens to discover it. "You go on holidays over there, a Toronto Bank manager explains, you draw a cheque on your local company and come back with cash in hand ...
Between sunrise and sunset on December 22, 1966, three days before Christmas, Seagrams succeeded in converting $17 million of taxable profits into non-taxable money simply by having them switched around from one to another of the many branches of the Bronfman empire ...
Imperial Oil.. .

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but his time has expired and unless he gets the unanimous consent of the House, he will not be able to carry on with his remarks.
Does the House agree to allow the hon. member to proceed with his remarks?
Agreed.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I also wish to thank my gracious colleagues for giving me the chance to complete my remarks because I was only beginning. I was surprised to hear that my time was up; however, I will try not to take advantage of the kindness of the House.
I go on with my quotation:
Imperial Oil... three directors and a secretary succeeded, from their homely little office in the Bermudas, in making a net profit of $35 million in less than five years! If that profit had been made in Canada rather than in the Bermudas, Imperial Oil would have paid $17.5 million additional taxes ...
Mr. Speaker, I could give many more examples just as down-to-earth and as Canadian; however, I have here a list of other Canadian companies that are slow in paying even the Canadian taxes they should pay.
Steel Company of Canada, Limited, have tax arrears of $149 million; Dominion Foundries and Steel, Limited, $101 million; Alcan Aluminum, $149 million; Aluminum Company of Canada, Limited, $139 million; International Nickel Company of Canada, Limited, $102 million; Imperial Oil Limited, $87 million; Domtar Limited, $53 million; (U.S.) Crown Zellerbach, $59 million; International Business Machines, $49 million; all the above mentioned compa-
May 27, 1976

nies have at the moment arrears each exceeding $50 million.
Mr. Speaker, a mere look at the Canadian taxation and monetary systems shows we must be blind not to realize or admit that they are sick. In 1963, we paid $1,431 million in interests on the public debt; in 1964, $1,546 million; in 1965, $1,675 million; in 1966, $1,862 million; in 1967, $2,081 million; in 1968, $2,391 million; in 1969, $2,774 million; in 1970, $3,183 million; the banks are making a remarkable progress; however, it is very surprising that they are not restricted to quotas; only the farmers who milk the cows are being imposed quotas. In 1971, $3,563 million; in 1972, $4,104; in 1973, $4,699; in 1974, $5,297; in 1975, over $4 billion and in 1976, $4,600.
Mr. Speaker, more than $45 billion. Canadian in Canadian taxes have been paid to big Canadian finance from 1963 to 1976. Indeed, 94 per cent of the interests on the national debt is paid directly to banks because 94 per cent of the bonds, the liabilities of the federal and provincial governments, are held by Canadian banks and 6 per cent is held by corporations or individuals. To those who would have me believe that if the Bank of Canada should finance interest-free the provincial, municipal, school and federal bonds, it is the low-income earners, the poor who will lose the interests, I say that it is utter nonsense when 94 per cent of the interests on the public debt is now paid only to banks in Canada. And at the same time, as Maclean magazine reported on December 15, 1975, the Royal Bank increased it s profits by $86 million, the Imperial Canadian Bank of Commerce, by $93 million, the Bank of Montreal by $81 million and the Bank of Nova Scotia, by $64 million.
Mr. Speaker, I could go on indefinitely. This budget clearly demonstrates that the Minister of Finance does not control finance in Canada. He should be the one to dictate the monetary policy to the Bank of Canada, and the chartered banks should follow the orders of the Bank of Canada following the recommendations of the Minister of Finance. Unfortunately, we find that 26 per cent of municipal budgets comes from property taxes and that 25.3 per cent of municipal budgets is assigned to interest payments to the chartered banks. I say again, because those figures are fantastic, that as reported in the Revue municipale du Quebec and other provincial magazines, 26 per cent of municipal budgets comes from property taxes and that 25.3 per cent is assigned to interest payments on the public debt, in other words there is a 1.3 per cent gap in municipal budgets between paid interests and collected property taxes.
Mr. Speaker, that is further evidence that our financial system is sick and the Social Credit Party has a solution to that problem. From 1973 to 1974, interests on the public debt, as I said, increased by 270.2 per cent. And as I just mentioned, interest charges for 1976-77 will reach approximately, as shown in the budget, $4.6 billion, that is $12.6 million a day, $500,000 an hour. Presently in Canada we pay $500,000 an hour in interest on the public debt, half a million an hour in interest, 24 hours a day, 365 days a year; that is what we pay to the banks to make money instead of using the Bank of Canada to finance our own public outlays as the Social Credit Party has always advocated in the House. This means that within 72 days, only with the
The Budget-Mr. Rondeau
interest on the public debt, we could wipe out the Olympic Games' debt that is causing so much fuss. We suggest that the Games' debt is of the order of $1 billion. This means that within 72 days, with the money given to the banks, because the banks finance our federal bounds we could save enough by using the Bank of Canada and without paying any interest to wipe out the public debt.
Mr. Speaker, in the province of Quebec, according to the Canadian Tax Foundation magazine Provincial and Municipal Finance 1975, on page 57, our international balance of payments on the automobile trade alone registered last year a deficit of nearly $5 billion:

Of Quebec's $3.4 billion in outstanding bonded debt at March 31, 1974-
The latest year for which I have figures is that ending March 31, 1974.

These figures are not up to date since they were released two years ago-

$2.9 billion was in negotiable bonds, $326.6 million in Quebec Savings Bonds, $131.6 million in federal employment loans and $35.6 million in Canada Pension Plan fund bonds. Negotiable bonded debt was payable in the following funds: $2,154.2 million in Canadian, $646.5 million in United States, $87.1 million in Federal Republic of Germany, $25.2 million in French, and $32.7 million in Japanese. Other loans outstanding included funds advanced by the federal government for Expo '67, $6.1 million and under the special areas agreement, $74.5 million; funds advanced by the Bank of Nova Scotia, $36.2 million. Other direct debt totalling $97.6 million included debt assumed by the province on behalf of the following entities: Montreal Metropolitan Boulevard, $39.5 million; universitarian institutions, $46.6 million; Quebec Municipal Commission for the settlement of school debts, $2.1 million; Institut de microbiologie et d'hygiene de Montreal, $4.4 million; Hopital St-Luc, Montreal, $4.7 million.

Mr. Speaker, I could carry on like this for a long time.
According to the same magazine, page 56, the provincial debts for the year ending March 31, 1974 had reached $11,406 million, indirect debts $17 billion, bonded debts assumed by provincial governments $15,203 million, and this does not include debts for education.
Mr. Speaker, I want to apologize and I am going to try to conclude as quickly as possible but I would like to draw your attention and that of my hon. colleagues on a book which has been published in November 1975 not, to my knowledge, by a Socred but by one of the best journalists in Canada, Mr. Peter C. Newman. I believe that several members of Parliament know of this book which is entitled The Canadian Establishment. This book presents an extraordinary documentation. Perhaps the organizations of our two traditional political parties will not find that it is in their interest to promote this book because it brings to light a wealth of information which is extremely valuable and which shows that in Canada we no longer live in a system of free enterprise, in a system of competition and in a system of private enterprise. This book makes one understand that one lives in a system of monopolies. Peter C. Newman mentions that 100 directors of Canadian banks control 1,022 companies: 35 Royal Bank directors control 471 companies, 31 Imperial Canadian Bank of Commerce directors control 317 companies, 16 Montreal Bank direc-

May 27, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Rondeau
tors control 178 companies, 4 Toronto-Dominion Bank directors control 56 companies, 14 directors of other banks control 180 companies. All told, 100 directors of various chartered banks control 1,022 Canadian companies.
I would like to quote him just on the subject of insurance to demonstrate that the Canadian banking system and the production system are one unique monopoly system with finance on one hand and on the other hand the same individuals acting in the consumer industry where for example one can see a Royal Bank director controlling Dominion Stores and Steinberg-production on one side and consumption on the other.
I want to quote what Peter C. Newman has to say about insurance. I say that this book is extremely valuable and I intend to use it often. On page 105, he writes:
The bank boards distill business power. Among them, the three hundred directors hold more than three thousand directorships of corporations with assets totalling $700 billion.
The bank directors are drawn from the corporate clusters interconnected with each of the banks. All but four of the top one hundred Canadian bank directors (ranked on the accompanying table according to the amount of the corporate assets with which they are involved) sit on the boards of the three largest banks. Each bank maintains special relationships with these client-directors and also with selected underwriters, law firms, auditing houses, trust and insurance companies. Some sixty-three bank directors sit on the boards of Canada's sixteen largest insurance firms, which control 83 per cent of their industry. Here is a tabulation of the extent of interlocking between banking and insurance boardrooms:

I shall mention only one: 14 banks directors sit on the board of the Sun Life Company. One could keep on reading this book: it is quite valuable. To prove the interlocking or the banking and production monopoly, we read this on page 115:
Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, I wonder if in fairness to those who are following the speaker would indicate for just how long he intends to continue with his speech?

I had intended to continue for another seven or eight minutes, if that does not displease my hon. colleagues too much. I would appreciate more time: there are so many other good things to read here that I could spare hon. members quite a lot of reading time.

The banks will not disclose any figures on how high a proportion of their credit is extended to their own directors. The only estimate ever published was in the report of the Royal Commission on Banking and Finance, which appeared in 1962. It stated that about 30 per cent of all authorized credit lines of $100,000 or more were "to directors, their firms or corporations of which they were officers or directors."

Mr. Speaker, if one keeps on reading that book, one gets a clear picture of the banks and the companies they control and soon realizes, as I did, that our system is one of monopoly, of production, and of finance from which we cannot extricate ourselves. When, for instance, workers go on strike to get a raise of, let us say, $20, after a one-week

strike and a settlement, they get their $20 increase in their pay envelope. The man who granted the increase in salary is the same one who controls, directly or indirectly, the cost of food at Dominion's or at Steinberg's. That is why, in our present-day system, strikes lead to absolutely nothing because we are part of an economic system where production and finance operate on a closed circuit. This is what the right hon. Prime Minister had to say about it on January 1 last, and I quote:

The free market system in Canada does not exist any more. [Translation]
He was absolutely right: the private enterprise system, the free enterprise system, does not exist any more in Canada. He was right. He is still right. But the same government deeply regrets that we have no competition system and no private bussinesses any more in Canada because they gave a few individuals the power to build an economic empire where finance, production and consumption are controlled.
Mr. Speaker, I regret that I do not have more time to continue my remarks because I have always been particularly interested in finance. I am convinced that it is not possible to make social and economic reforms without giving first our attention to the area of finance. Today, the federal governement, the government which is or should be sovereign, is at the mercy of financial instututions and in his book entitled The Canadian Establishment, Peter C. Newman proves that this system exists today. Thus, it is not by passing petty legislation and by changing some taxes that we are going to correct the situation.
For example, some years ago, a U.S. Senate subcommittee was asked to make an inquiry on trusts, monopolies and finance and at the end of the inquiry, the chairman of this committee, the Chief Justice of the U.S. Supreme Court said there was only one monopoly, namely the monopoly of credit; then we realized that Peter C. Newman said in his book that with one hand we extend credit to companies, generous credit through banks at a given moment this credit is withdrawn or restricted as far as these companies are concerned. It says in the book that banks grant credit to the tune of $100,000 or more to their own managers in order to purchase the controlling shares of the company. Problems have been created through the use of credit, the debit balance of bank accounts.
Mr. Speaker, I would have fantastic examples to give in Canada, but I know that at the present time in the province of Quebec a company must accept to be controlled by the banks or go into bankruptcy. Banks have a 40 per cent control over that company which has become a multinational company. The chairman of that company is reluctant to yield the controlling shares of the company to a group very well known in Montreal, Power Corporation, which wants to take over that company, and we know that Power Corporation has tremendous connections with the Royal Bank, as Peter C. Newman mentions in his book.
What struck me in the book by Peter C. Newman, Mr. Speaker, and I would not like to displease my hon. friends opposite, was to find out that most of the Anti-Inflation Board officials were at one time executives of Power Cor-
May 27, 1976

poration in the province of Quebec or in other subsidiaries controlled by Power Corporation.
Mr. Speaker, I do not understand how executives who were under the authority of Power Corporation can serve the interests of the Canadian people unless Power Corporation, through the AIB, wants to control small businesses so as to take them over eventually through the Royal Bank, which is behind Power Corporation.

Mr. Speaker, I rose on a point of order to ask the previous speaker, the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau), how long he would be because possibly this is one opportunity we should take to revise our rules. I was in a similar position on another occasion when the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) asked for a few minutes in order to finish his speech. At that time he continued for half an hour. The hon. member for Shefford took another 20 minutes. In fact he spoke longer than the representative of the official opposition when that gentleman made his remarks.
The hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Salts-man), when he began his speech, said that he would forgo the luxury of rebutting the previous speaker, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens). I will give the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge credit for producing a speech in which he made some positive suggestions even if I do not agree with them. I shall not go over them simply because my experience is that socialists act completely differently when in office. This is well illustrated by the socialist governments in this country.
However, I do wish to deal with the remarks made by the hon. member for York-Simcoe. This is a luxury I do not think I can afford to forgo. His remarks were so full of platitudes, and so on, that at times I found it difficult even to credit them to the hon. member for York-Simcoe. He said that it is hard-working Canadians who pay for the government's spending program. I find that a little hard to take. Who else but Canadians will pay for the government's spending program, whether it be the spending program of this federal government or of any provincial government? It is a nice pat expression to say that it is the taxpayers who will pay. Whether it be the consumers or the taxpayers, someone must pay for whatever the government's level of spending may be.
He then went on to mention what he said amounted to $1 billion in spending cuts. Let us analyze some of these cuts. He talked about energy price increases. He spoke of the $1.05 and the 70 cents. He mentioned the ten cents levy put on by the government. He did not say that he objected to this.
He did not say that he supported one price. He did not say, if he was supporting one price, how he would set it up. He did not indicate whether he thought this was a good thing. He mentioned that we are spending $1.8 billion in price support in respect of oil in this country. He did not say whether he thought it would be preferable to let the price for gasoline and heating oil rise to the world price so that we would not have to subsidize gasoline and heating
The Budget-Mr. Herbert
oil in this country. That would be one method by which we could save 1.8 billion. He did not mention that.
You should read the speech. You missed the point.

He talked of foreign markets. We know they are there. He did not make any specific suggestions about how to get greater access to those markets. He did not mention the competitive factor or that perhaps we should subsidize our exports to increase our exports. He just said the markets are there. Of course they are there. We could sell to them if we are competitive. One of the reasons we have not been able to sell is that our competitive position has somewhat decreased.
Then he had a real nice pat expression. He said that the family farm is an efficient unit of production. This should be good for getting some farm votes, so I shall repeat it. The family farm is an efficient unit of production. He mentioned that four tenths of the capital regulation is in the private sector and following that, because he wants to see capital generated, he spoke against profit control. I repeat that: he spoke against profit control.
I want every salaried worker in this country whose salary presently is under the wage guidelines of this country to take note that the hon. member for York-Simcoe spoke against profit control.
He wants to stimulate the economy to provide more jobs in the private sector. He did not mention the amount of money we should spend. He studiously avoided talking about any more spending although he mentioned several programs which would require an input of dollars in order for them to be effective.
He then mentioned the Post Office. This is interesting. He mentioned some figures, just as he has so often at committee meetings. I cannot miss this opportunity to talk about the hon. member for York-Simcoe and his performance in committees. He is what I call a flitter. Like a butterfly which goes from flower to flower the hon. member flits from committee to committee. On some occasions he will attend a committee meeting and make a proposal because, after all, as the official spokesman for the official opposition he must show that he has studied the estimates. He will make some amendments to cut the estimates to lower government spending.
I shall not read from the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence of the committee but I would refer any interested member to the meeting of the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs of May 4 when the hon. member suggested a cut in the budget of the minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald). I shall not go into all the details, but there is an interesting point to this. He took a look at the estimates and made an assumption which was indicated to be false assumption. He then found himself in the ridiculous position of being a financial critic notwithstanding the fact that he really had not done his homework.
Balderdash.

The next item he mentioned was the $300 million that has to be raised by Crown corporations such as, for example, Canadian National. I did not really understand him. Was the hon. member suggesting that he was in
May 27, 1976

The Budget-Mr. Herbert
favour of having all the money for the Crown corporations raised by the Minister of Finance? After all he should be consistent. We should follow the same procedure for all Crown corporations. Would this not in some way dig into the independence of the Crown corporations? Would it not be contrary to what we are trying to do, for instance, in respect of Air Canada by separating it from Canadian National and making it independent? Would it not be wrong under those circumstances for a Crown corporation to be reliant on the government for its financing by having the government raise the money for Crown corporations?
He mentioned another little cut of $90 million. He wants to get rid of all the outside contracts. This has been the favourite theme of the Tory party. He says we can save all of that because we are going to improve the efficiency of the public service. Presumably all that work will be done by our present public servants with no increase in salary, and nobody extra will be brought in. It will be an additional load on these public servants. In the next breath he says that he would take another $50 million out of the public service-I do not know how. Will he reduce their salaries and have fewer bodies doing more work? He did not say, but anyway there is a nice, neat $90 million worth of extra work to be done by the public service and they will get $50 million less for doing it.
His next remark concerned the number of ministers. He does not want 29 ministers, he wants fewer. It occurred to me that not so long ago there was a Tory convention at which it was proposed that there be more ministries. I wonder has there been a change once again in the Conservative policy, or is this just the idea of the hon. member for York-Simcoe. If we are going to have fewer ministers- which is perhaps not a bad idea and I myself have suggested a different structure-if we have to get rid of some, which ones should be eliminated and which ones should we put together? No mention was made of that. The hon. member just said that there are too many ministers, that we should get rid of some, but he made no positive suggestions on this.
Then he went on to the subject of spending. He is going to let everybody share $350 million. We should give everybody a tax break, he says. That is a good one. I do not know where they money is to come from. He says it would come from some millions of dollars that he has decided to cut off spending, but as I listened to, item by item, I did not find any moneys in actual dollars. This was another of these figments of the imagination without any follow through. Despite that, the hon. member would like to distribute some of these moneys, and he would give a tax break to those earnings $16,000 and less. He is also going to give $100 million to the private sector to increase research. He did not go on to do much explaining about this, so I will put a question to him.
The pharmaceutical industry in this country has had some problems with research work. Is he suggesting that it might be a good idea to infuse some of his $100 million in the pharmaceutical industry so that perhaps this industry could do some of the important research that is presently being done in other countries, specifically in Ireland, where they get a better tax break than in this country, and

also in the United States? He did not say, but at any rate he is keen on giving the private sector $100 million.
In the next breath he is willing to give another $25 million for medical research. That is a good one, of course, because everybody wants to find cures and prevent diseases, as he mentioned, and this ties in very well with the demonstration which we witnessed here last week at which, incidentally, this particular group was asking for $6.4 million. It occurs to me that if we are going to be popular, then why limit this to $25 million? There does not seem to be any sense in the figures. It does not tie in with anybody,s request. It might be one way of saying, "Let us give a handout to everybody while we are giving money away, let everyone share in the bonanza."
The hon. member for York-Simcoe mentioned small businessmen. He did not say what benefits were put in the budget for small businessmen but he mentioned the horrors of filling out government forms. His way of solving this problem is not to suggest a specific form which may be unnecessary. Incidentally, may I say here that to every businessman who has written me on this subject I put these questions: What specific form do you object to? Will you send me a copy of that form so that I can explain to you why it has to be filled in and can get your response? I can say that although I have posed this question to every businessman who has complained to me about filling in forms, I have still to receive the first form.
In the next sentence the hon. member for York-Simcoe went on to complain about interest rates which are 3 per cent higher in Canada than in the United States, he maintains. He did not say anything about the fact that we need capital in Canada, nor did he say that the reason for higher interest rates is that money is coming into Canada and that interest rates have to be higher here than in the United States to attract the capital we need. He did not mention if there is a real effect on, for example, construction.
We have heard a lot said about construction and interest rates in this country, but it is quite interesting that although mortgage interest rates in Canada at present are nearly 50 per cent higher than rates in the United States, housing starts in Canada per capita are twice as great as in the United States. The United States, with all its wealth and power, is only building shelter at half the rate on a per capita basis that we are in Canada.
I should mention another thing also because there has been another Tory theme proposed many times, namely, that mortgage interest be deductible for tax purposes. It is deductible in the United States. How is it, since interest rates are so much lower and since the interest on mortgages is deductible for tax purposes, that there has not been the stimulus in housing that he seems to indicate would occur if the same situation prevailed in Canada? I suggest that there is not too much wrong with the housing program in Canada at present. The government's housing programs have been highly successful, and are certainly nothing to be ashamed of in this country in so far as the number of houses we have built in recent years is concerned.
The hon. member for York-Simcoe, the official Conservative financial critic, was complaining in a Toronto Star report on March 26, 1975, that the November, 1974,
May 27, 1976

budget did not provide a sufficient stimulus to the economy and that a new budget is needed. "It is needed now more than ever," he stated. During the debate on the June, 1975, budget in which a stimulus was injected into the economy, the same hon. member contended that major cuts should be made in government spending so as to reduce both the government's budget deficit and its cash deficit, which would of course reduce the amount of economic stimulus.
Up to the time of the May 25, 1976, budget the same Conservative spokesman continued to call for an imposition of restrictive fiscal and monetary policies, but after the budget the hon. member for York-Simcoe appeared to want to go both ways at the same time. He contended on television that there should have been a cut in government spending, a cut in taxes for those in lower income brackets, and a cut in the deficit.
That is what I said today.

In starting the debate on Thursday night he criticized the budget because it failed to make a commitment to provide real economic growth this year of 6 per cent and to bring about a reduction in employment.
What is wrong with that?

May I ask the hon. member to explain by what sleight of hand he proposes to pull off this amazing piece of fiscal magic whereby government spending is reduced, taxes are reduced, and the government's deficit is reduced, but the growth of output and employment is increased?
Because the private sector is given a chance.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It being six o'clock, I do now leave the chair until eight o'clock tonight.
At six o'clock the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, when I stopped at six o'clock I was pointing out that the totally contradictory position espoused by the hon. member for York-Simcoe, the financial spokesman for the Official Opposition-I notice he has disappeared since the supper break-is the ultimate in economic nonsense. Apart from some brief reversals of position in the past the Conservatives have advocated the adoption of tight fiscal and monetary policies since 1974, from the time the economy was heading into a slump as a result of world-wide recession, and throughout that period. Now that the economy is pulling out of recession the Conservatives seem to be advocating the adoption of restrictive expansionary economic policies.
The Budget-Mr. Herbert
If the government had followed the course advocated by the Conservatives over the past few years, Canada would undoubtedly have suffered a more severe and prolonged recession than that of any other major industrial country, and unemployment today would certainly be at the double digit level.
The latest position of the Tories seems to involve jamming down hard on the accelerator and the brakes at one and the same time so as to achieve the best of all possible worlds. They call for the injection of massive stimulus to hasten the growth of output and employment. If there was any lesson to be learned from the hard experience of the earlier years of the 1970's it was that trying to push the economy ahead too hard and too fast only laid the groundwork for future inflation and recession.
Let me mention, in the few moments remaining to me, some of the main spending programs not touched upon by the hon. member for York-Simcoe. Some two thirds of the government spending programs which he has been criticizing in such broad and general terms today involve money transferred into the pockets of individuals-such as old age pensions, veterans' pensions, subsidies for bread, or money transferred into the pockets of other levels of government. Moneys are transferred as a result of the payments made by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, and huge sums are spent in equalization payments. I recognize that the hon. member for York-Simcoe comes from the rich province of Ontario, but he did not mention whether he approves or disapproves of the transfer of these federal funds to the "have not" provinces; he did not mention whether he approves or disapproves of the large sums already put into the housing programs to increase even further the building of housing that is presently taking place. He made no mention, for example, of the large sums being spent on training programs for the unemployed.
I note, for example, that Canada has had and continues to have the most rapidly growing labour force in the western world. Each year over half a million young people leave school and enter the labour force. Once there they experience major employment difficulties-younger workers account for nearly half our unemployed.
Our adult training program is now considered one of the largest in the world on a per capital expenditure basis. In 1975 over 80,000 people, a number equal to 2 per cent of the labour force, successfully competed training. Expenditures on the program in 1975 amounted to more than $475 million. Does the hon. member for York-Simcoe approve or disapprove?
When he was talking about the cost of the Post Office he did not mention that only 9 per cent of all the material going in and out of the Post Office is private mail. He did not mention the multimillion dollars subsidy that goes to business as a result of the Post Office deficit. He did not suggest that we should substantially increase postal rates to remove that subsidy to the businesses he has been supporting so well.

Just run it efficiently.

May 27, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Herbert
He did not mention the large sums of money for cultural spending. He did not suggest it might be a good idea to cut back on cultural programs.
Do you?

He did not suggest that we are spending too much money, although some people think that we may be. Only 11 per cent of the total television viewing time is through CBC channels.
He did not mention the large sums of money being spent on foreign aid for the Third World and CIDA.
He did not mention one of the favourite whipping boys of the official opposition, the bilingualism program, particularly in view of the recent comments of Mr. Spicer. Of course these moneys are being spent to try to make Anglophones bilingual.
He did not mention welfare and all the moneys transferred to the provinces. He did not mention that his party seemed to be opposing some limitation on the moneys being spent on these programs by the federal government. He did not mention indexing, which is one of the reasons why the federal government expenditures are increasing. He did not say whether he approved or disapproved of the fact that some of our best programs, pension programs, for example, are indexed. He did not mention specifically any of the government programs in a fashion in which we could judge whether the Conservatives were for or against them.
One of the things quite obviously we have to be very careful of is labour cost's going up and making us less competitive. Figures show that in the last five years in the United States total labour costs per hour have gone up by some 43 per cent; in Canada they have gone up by some 77 per cent. This indicates that whereas we had an edge on labour rates five years ago, today we are lagging behind. Figures show that on a per unit basis we are running 3 per cent or 4 per cent higher than the United States.
In introducing the budget the Minister of Finance said:
The world economy is launched on recovery from the worst recession since the great depression of the 1930's. As an exporting nation, Canada was bound to be affected by the slump among its trading partners.
Yet the performance of the Canadian economy during this period in terms of output, employment and real incomes has been better than virtually every other industrial nation.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, the Tory party are just preachers of gloom and doom.
Everyone has read negative comments in the mass media. Different interest groups have adopted a defeatist attitude. The government urges everyone to stop being pessimistic. To demand that the anti-inflation program be abolished even before it is applied, to be on the look out for anything that can discredit it, and to break off talks with the government, are clearly negative attitudes.
The government urges everyone to consider objectively the economic situation of Canada, the problem of inflation, the inequities it creates, the groups it penalizes, and the means we have to deal with it. The government has warned that the evils of inflation can only get worse if effective measures are not adopted. It was not afraid of becoming unpopular when it warned that the program

might involve a degree of rough justice and that it might cause hardship in some instances.
The government has shown leadership, Mr. Speaker. It invites everyone else to do the same. Forget the critics and the pessimists. Be positive. Be proud we have so much for which we can be thankful. A constructive attitude will speed the return to an inflation-free, full employment economy.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to start by saying that from the remarks of the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert), the people might wonder whether the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) is the Minister of Finance. Unfortunately for Canadians, that day may come!
After bringing down five budgets, one of which was rejected by Parliament, Mr. John Turner resigned as finance minister. During his mandate as finance minister, the real economic growth dropped from about 6 per cent to near zero. The trade deficit increased tenfold. Inflation jumped from 4.8 per cent to 10.8 per cent. Over 145,000 additional workers found themselves jobless and federal expenditures doubled.
After putting up with so many economic troubles, Canadians were entitled to expect an improvement in their economic position. Hemmed in by the limits of the antiinflation program, the people wanted to see the light at the end of the recession tunnel. Canada needed renewed confidence in the future. And good federal leadership could have given it to them. That will be for 1978.
In his first budget speech since he became Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) he showed he was just as incapable as his predecessor. Instead of alleviating the problem of inflation and unemploment he Minister of Finance only promises a situation that is barely improved, that is an unperceivable improvement in the rate of inflation and a rate of unemployment that will still remain high. Instead of taking Canada out of the recession the minister proposes a pious game whereby increased trade with other countries, more specifically the United States, will put an end to the recession. He therefore sheds his responsibility to work at maintaining the rate of real growth of the economy. And instead of inspiring trust by showing federal leadership, all the minister provides is uncertainty about the intentions of the federal government and total renouncement of its leadership in the fight against inflation.
This budget is impregnated with inability to meet the expectations of Canadians. Government expenditures are a good example although the paper "Fight against inflation" suggested federal expenditures would not grow at a greater rate than economic growth. The information contained in the budget indicates an increase in federal budgetary expenditures of 16.3 per cent for the fiscal year 1977 over the fiscal year 1976 while the economic growth for the year 1976 will be 14 per cent.
The minister managed to reduce his estimates on expenditure increases to 14 per cent during that period using those very same obscure accounting practices made famous by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien). The increase in federal expenditures was minimized with
May 27, 1976

two kinds of subterfuges. First, expenditures for the fiscal year 1976 rose by $725 million more than the final budgetary estimates brought in by the President of the Treasury Board. That increase was not caused by unforeseen costs but rather a voluntary policy of stepped-up non-budgetary expenditures.
Second, this government excluded from its books the financial needs of two Crown corporations to arrive at the illusory saving of $300 million. If those little games with figures had not taken place, that is if the whole activity of supposedly cut back non-budgetary loans put back in time or destined to disappear under another method had been properly charged to the accounts, federal expenditures would have soared by more than 16 per cent.
The minister wanted to prove to the Canadian people that he had nothing to do with this excessive spending, which he did not say to Canadians. To clear himself, he had to confuse the figures. The 16 per cent increase in federal spending stands in sharp contrast against the restraint applied by other sectors of the economy. For instance, let us consider the labour sector which is restricted to a maximum wage increase of 12 per cent; let us consider the business community which is forced by these estimates to limit its profits to 85 per cent compared with previous levels; let us consider the provinces which keep their spending increases at 11 per cent; let us consider the Bank of Canada which succeeds in maintaining the money growth at about 10 per cent. The financial critic for the Progressive Conservative party, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), in his preliminary remarks on the budget, summarized the situation in more or less the following terms:
Although the federal government is asking all Canadians to participate in the anti-inflation program, it has carefully excluded itself from participation. This is another example of the lack of leadership of the part of the government and deceived of expectations: the failure by the Minister of Finance to commit himself to correct the losses in the economic growth which Canada has experienced for the last two years. In terms of long run economic yield, the real GNP was $7.7 billion below potential in 1975, after allowing for inflation. Such a decrease in relation to potential means per capita a loss of $339 in real GNP. Faced with such a considerable loss, all the minister of Finance has to say he hopes trade improvements will bring actual growth up to 5 per cent this year. We hear from him no long term commitment for compensating the losses faced by all Canadians.
In fact, he ventured no growth projection for the coming years. Because the economy was allowed to bog down in such a dangerous way, Canadians have experienced tremendous losses in potential jobs, revenue, productivity and well-being. If nothing is done now to recoup those losses, they may very well become of a permanent nature. That the minister should acknowledge those losses without doing anything to straighten them out is one of the great tragedies in this budget.
There are relatively few measures of a true budgetary nature in this budget. As a matter of form, some tax reductions were included for the average taxpayer, and the
The Budget-Mr. Lavoie
tax burden of small and medium firms was somewhat alleviated. Some changes were also made for energy conservation purposes. This is all very well, but the bulk of these measures certainly have no real significance, considering that they represent a reduction of only $75 million in government revenue, whereas the total revenue increase will reach $4.5 million for the current year.
Once all the rhetoric is taken out, this budget offers Canadians nothing to indicate that the federal government is ready to practice restraint. Nothing for recouping the losses in actual growth, nothing for housing, nothing for agriculture, nothing for productivity, nothing in the way of jobs, nothing to eliminate regional disparities. In other words, discounting the bad news in the budget, one is justified to ask, as did the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Clark), why the Minister went to the trouble of introducing it.
I would now like to comment on some of the more specific aspects of the current economic situation, which are of great concern to me. The first aspect is unemployment. There are now upwards of 760,000 Canadians unemployed. During the year 1975, we had an average of 697,000 unemployed. The fact that more and more Canadians become jobless is in my view a new and very inauspicious trend.
Indeed, since December 1975, almost 50,000 more Canadians have been looking for a job. Will this figure grow? I do not want to sound like an alarmist, but I am afraid it will. In his budget speech, the minister said he expected that more than 250,000 jobs will be created in 1976. This figure seems very impressive. I feel I still have to ask the following questions. The first one is important enough: how can the government increase the number of jobs when, in the Department of Manpower and Immigration and in Statistics Canada, people are being laid off and told there is a lack of work. I wonder if those people will be put on the minister's list of new jobs; I hope so in any case.
And in another aspect, I would like to ask the minister in what industry, in what province, these jobs will be created. And moreover, a question of so great importance: will these jobs be enough to allow first-time job seekers to find employment? Where will these jobs be created? The budget speech does not give any indication of it, nor does the reply given by the minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) to our spokesman in financial matters. The minister does not know either. Where are those incentives in the budget which would allow industry to generate jobs? Certainly not in the anti-inflation program where it is stated that profits should be maintained at 85 per cent of their proceeding level. Certainly not in this insignificant cut of $30 million allowed to small and middle-size industries.
Those jobs may come with export industries which the minister expects will experience a miraculous recovery in the coming year but export industries expected to recover during the year are those which export our resources and not our manufactured goods. It is a well-known fact that industries in the primary sector contribute far less than those in the secondary sector to job creation. This is why I am convinced that little employment will be directly creat-

May 27, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Lavoie
ed by the recovery of industries which export our resources.
Can we expect any recovery from Canadian industries exporting manufactured goods? I hope so, as this area can certainly be largely improved, but the minister has already informed Canadians that the manufacturing industry has lost all competitiveness in the international field. An illustration in the economic review of the Department of Finance clearly demonstrates today that even manufacturers are not competitive. How could this industry create employment when it is not competitive?
I am not enough of an expert in the financial field to be in position to criticize the minister's forecasts concerning job creation. I have my doubts and I think they are justified. What I ask the minister is to explain how he can expect to create 250,000 new jobs considering the present economic situation and the proposed budgetary policies. I wish, and I think that the Canadian people wish it too, to be convinced of the validity of his projections and of the fact that the minister does not raise false hopes in the minds of Canadians.
In what areas of Canada are those jobs to be created? Are they going to be created in the wealthy and affluent provinces? This will not solve the problem of regional disparities? In my own province, Quebec, there are 224,000 unemployed accounting for 8.3 percent of the manpower. Even if a third of the 250,000 new jobs which are to be created this year were directed to the province of Quebec tomorrow morning, the unemployment rate in my province would still be over 5 percent.
Such an unemployment rate would still be unacceptable in my province, but even more so is the fact that Quebec will probably go through another year with an unemployment rate much higher than the national average. If the minister has the courage to tell Canadians what industries will create these jobs, I hope he will tell us as well in what provinces these jobs will be opened. I want to hear from the minister whether the inflation and recession that took place recently in this country have increased regional disparities.
I asked earlier if 250,000 new jobs would be enough to prevent the unemployment rate from rising if not to reduce it. He says that all these jobs will be created but he does not say anything about the number of new workers who will enter the labour market. If we knew the growth rate of the labour force, we could say whether there will be more people searching for a job than new jobs created. A projection of the growth of the labour force provided by the Conference Board in Canada referred to a little more than 310,000 people. On this basis, it is obvious that the minister tries to tell us that even though 250,000 new jobs will be created, 310,000 people be looking for work, which means a net increase of 60,000 unemployed people. This means that the unemployment rate will go up in 1976. However, in his budget speech, page 32, the minister states that "the rate of unemployment will continue the recent level trend in the near term". Can he explain this statement? After all, the livelihood and welfare of several thousands of people are at stake and I do not think he should play statistical games with the Canadian people.
I would like to deal with another matter in my speech today, in relation with the above. There is nothing in this

budget that will assist the workers, the backbone of our economy and our greater resource. According to the guidelines brought forward by the present administration in its "Fight against inflation", workers wages are frozen at a maximum increase of 12 per cent. According to the minister, page 11, "compliance with the program is widespread". Well, the worker is therefore following the wage control and showing personal restraint. But what is he given in exchange? In this budget, the minister is only providing for another $15 million in deductions for child care costs. It also offers $60 million in cutbacks for those who make important investments in retirement pension plans, but how many average Canadians can, according to their salaries, take advantage of such a policy?
Most Canadian consumers must face higher provincial sales taxes, higher property rates, sickness insurance costs, education taxes, and other costs. I do not blame the federal Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) if the provinces need revenues, but he must surely notice that higher taxes reduce the net salary of the worker. Why does this budget provide no advantage to the worker to incite him to comply with the salary freeze? Not only is there no advantage for the worker but the worker whose salary is freezed must tolerate a 16 per cent increase in government expenses. The rules of the federal government apply to everyone except itself.
This budget is highly incomplete and much too shy; that is the least one can say. I am sure that in their speeches my colleagues will know how to demonstrate all its inadequacies.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal with a last subject before I resume my seat. I would like to join all those who protested against the cutbacks this government made in the funds allocated to medical research. Even for a government which says it is interested in cutting its expenses, such a cut makes no sense at all and it is like going backward.
The present administration complained many times about soaring health care costs. In my opinion, it is more reasonable to spend money to try to find the best means of protecting health than to cure diseases which could have been prevented. Obviously such an approach would give results in the long run. At least it would be a slightly more humane and more enlightened way of dealing with such an important and vital field as medical research.
As I said in my previous remarks, this budget is a source of disappointment. It contains innumerable shortcomings and, on the whole, creates only confusion. The least we can expect from the minister is that he clarify the misunderstanding that surround his estimates. When the minister has the opportunity again to take part in this debate, or when his colleagues speaks, I hope they will tell us where all these jobs come from. Will there be enough of them? I hope they will point out those aspects of the budget and concern themselves with the workers. I shall not be the only one to listen to the answers of the minister.
The people in my riding, in my province and in my country will do the same. Suffice it to say that the impression the people are left with today, about the budget, impression that I share with them, corresponds to a large extent to what Claude Ryan of Le Devoir said about it in his editorial this morning, and I quote;
May 27, 1976

Mr. Macdonald took care not so specify what amounts he hopes to recuperate through the new restrictions he will be proposing for eligibility for unemployment insurance benefits. One must wonder, however, whether it might not have been preferable to try to recover those amounts from the categories of high-income taxpayers who have all sorts of means at their disposal for sheltering themselves against the consequences of inflation. From that specific aspect, Mr. Macdonald's budget is disappointing. No other measure having otherwise been put forth to improve the lot of the small taxpayer, one must conclude that he will be, during the coming year, the main scapegoat of the federal government fiscal policy.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to give a little praise to the minister-
Not too much, of course.
Just a little.

The minister has included a few things in his budget which the party I support has been advocating for some time. In particular I should like to refer to the adjustments to the unemployment insurance plan with special emphasis on the extension of the qualifying period from eight weeks to twelve weeks.
Down in the maritimes you would not say that.
That is where he went wrong.

I sense some opposition in the House, not only from my left but from across the way. Another thing I welcome in the budget is the removal of the dividend freeze and the increase in the deduction allowable under retirement savings plans. Lest the minister think we are altogether in favour of these changes I should like to make a comment about the ending of the dividend freeze. This is something I have advocated on a number of occasions and I should like to think the minister was listening sympathetically.
Large numbers of Canadians rely on dividends to a greater or lesser extent as a source of income. The minister could never explain how he expected retired people living on dividends to cope with the rising cost of living, which was not frozen, while relying on dividends which were frozen. I am sure pensioners will welcome the change, particularly if the minister can bring down the rate of inflation to something like 8 per cent, as he suggests he can. Of course the problem affects more than just pensioners-it affects pension plans in general, and practically every working person in Canada has an interest in a pension plan. I might add that practically every pension plan has an interest in the profitability of Canadian companies.
There is a factor in the dividend proposal, however, which I cannot understand. It ties in with the rate of profits which will be allowed. Corporations were allowed to earn 95 per cent of their previous taxable incomes but the proportion is now to be lowered to 85 per cent; profits must not rise above 85 per cent of profits during the base period. So we are now in the position of saying to business, "You cannot make as much money as you used to, but you
The Budget-Mr. Clarke
may increase your dividends." I cannot see how a businessman acting in a proper manner can reconcile those two requirements.
Furthermore, having been a businessman before I came here, I have difficulty in understanding how a corporation is expected to control its profits. Volume plays a tremendous part in the profit picture. As one example I might cite the Bricklin Automobile Company; it certainly had no problem in controlling its profits because it did not make any, so the regulations restricting profits were not difficult for that company to comply with. But take the case of Chrysler Corporation-I recognize that this is an American company but I am sure there are many similar Canadian examples. The new models they put out in 1976, the Volare and Aspen, proved to be their salvation; the cars sold like hot cakes. How anyone can expect to control profits when a company is fortunate in hitting upon a hot sales object such as that, I cannot imagine.
With regard to the changes in the pension plan contributions, may I say they are certainly to be recommended and were long overdue. The pension plan legislation was introduced in 1970. I believe, and the limits set at that time have been unchanged ever since, so the increase of roughly 14 per cent was overdue. However, I would remind the minister that there is an extremely limited market for an improvement of this kind. For most Canadians the question is how to arrange to have a few extra dollars left over to invest in anything, let alone to put $3,500 or more into a registered retirement savings or a pension plan.
My hon. friend from York-Simcoe noted the fact that this budget would leave the little man bearing the burden of taxation. He quoted statistics which clearly support that contention. I should like to give another example because I feel the government does not understand the problems of the little man.
A few days ago we were debating the estimates of the Post Office Department in the House. At that time the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) told us that the cost of first class mail would rise 50 per cent over the next year or so. He said that the average Canadian wrote only four or five letters anyway so the cost to him would be only 8 or 10 cents every year. I made a quick calculation before putting some questions to the minister and it seemed to me the increase in the postal rates was likely to be some $200 million. Dividing that sum among the population I found it came to more like $10 per Canadian than 10 cents. Put this into a family context and we shall probably find that the average cost of the projected increases will be more like $50 a year rather than $10, or 8 or 10 cents.
What about the business mail?

That is a point which was stressed by the Postmaster General. He said that 80 per cent of postal costs were paid by 20 per cent of the customers and, of course, he was referring to the business community. What he failed to explain was that the business community will pass the increase along to its customers. Business has a way of doing this because, after all, business has no money of its own-it only gets its money from outside. There is no other source of funds. Furthermore the increased costs to corporations are deducted in arriving at taxable income.

May 27, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Clarke
A sum, which could be estimated at approximately $100 million roughly as a part of that increase in the postal rates, will be a cost to the taxpayers through reduced revenue to the government because taxable incomes will be lower until the cost actually is passed on to the customers. When the minister was questioned on this he agreed- the error was 100 times; it was not 8 cents or 10 cents but $10 per Canadian-that my analysis was probably correct but said in defence that the Post Office deficit was also paid for by the little man. I will have something more to say about what is or is not paid for by the little man later on.
It is interesting that members who sit to my left and members who sit opposite do not understand that all the government's money is taken from the little man, the taxpayer. They do not seem to understand that the government has no funds of its own to spend and furthermore that the corporations have no money of their own to spend. It is all taxpayers' money. It is the individual who pays.
Another aspect in dealing with the little man is that wages in this country are not expected to rise by more than 12 per cent in the current year. Personal exemptions are indexed at a rate which I understand is 11.3 per cent, which is designed to take care of most of the effect of the increased wages. This too reflects on the tax burden of the individual. Yet the minister in his speech on budget night indicated that the yield from direct taxes on individuals is expected to increase by 26 per cent. I cannot reconcile how a small increase in wages of 12 per cent, which is supposed to be offset by the increase in personal exemptions, will result in an increased yield of 26 per cent.
We can look at that from another unexplained point of view. The minister said that the gross national product was expected to increase by between 14 per cent and 15 per cent in the current year. I cannot relate that to an expected increase in direct taxes on individuals of 26 per cent. I feel there is something wrong with the arithmetic the minister used in respect of his budget.
The hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) referred to his suggested cutting of expenses and the suggested allocation of those savings. He indicated that $100 million should be applied to the relief of those Canadians who earn under $8,000 a year. The latest figures available in respect of personal income taxes are for 1973. They reveal that Canadians who earn-and this is the gross rather than the taxable income-an income of $4,000 or less paid $104 million in the form of personal income taxes in 1973. Those Canadians who earn what both the provincial government and the federal government declare is the minimum wage earn at the federal minimum wage of $2.90 per hour $6,000 per year, and at the provincial minimum rate of $2.65 an hour earn an annual income of $5,500. Yet in 1973 those who earned $4,000 a year paid $100 million a year in the form of personal income taxes.
There are other measures in this budget to which I would refer as housekeeping measures. At least I did refer to some of them in that manner until today. One example of what I call housekeeping measures would be the control of abuses in the operation of charities in Canada. I thought it was quite revealing that there are estimated to be 35,000 charities in Canada and that the annual contribution taken
in by these exceeds $1 billion. I think it is fair to observe at the same time that the government makes an involuntary and indirect payment through forgiven taxes to that $1 billion since the contributors to the charitable organizations deduct the contribution in computing the tax payable. Of course the tax bracket would have to be taken into consideration. However, a large amount is involved.
Further there is the reduction of the capital cost allowances in respect of leased equipment, electrical generation equipment, and advertising signs. There are also increased write-offs allowed on roads, computer hardware, taxi cabs and a few other items. Today representatives of the leasing industry say that the result of their inability to make the normal deduction for capital cost allowance to which they had been accustomed will result in higher leasing rates. Very little arithmetic is required to figure out where the higher leasing rate will be directed in order to finance this change in the budget.
Another factor that has developed today is the higher tax on construction companies which operate heavy equipment. Because the capital cost allowance on heavy equipment has been reduced, the payments that heavy equipment operators receive for their work will be higher in the future in order that they can cover the higher tax bill that will result from the fact that they cannot reduce their incomes by way of capital cost allowance in the way in which they were accustomed.
Another housekeeping measure would be the increased deduction for child care. I am certain the minister experienced much pressure in this regard. Certainly there were inequalities and inequities existent in the realm of child care. The adjustment in respect of deductions for disabled persons and students probably was overdue.
Another area that has been given a great deal of attention by the minister involves the advantages of small business. The rate of 25 per cent on small business incomes is to be increased from $100,000 to $150,000 a year with an accumulated maximum of $750,000 instead of $500,000. I was disappointed to note that there is still no relief for small corporations which, for some reason or other, are deemed not to be in active business. If a business is deemed to be an inactive or investment-type business the small-business rate does not apply and it is taxed at the normal rate of 50 per cent. There seems to be no attempt to plug the loophole which allows a small active business that has achieved an accumulated income of $750,000 to be wound up, another company started up and permits the new one to receive more relief.
I think it would be more appropriate if the minister had given some kind of relief to small businessmen who for some reason cannot afford or do not wish to incorporate. If you operate a business without the benefit of incorporation, no matter how much income you realize you pay at your normal personal rate and there is no way in which you can accumulate funds for the expansion of the business. Many small businessmen feel they cannot justify the costs of incorporation and they have to go along with the rules as they were before.
There is another matter in connection with small business in Canada which needs attention and which was ignored by the minister in this budget, and that is relief for the businessman who operates an unincorporated business

May 27, 1976

and who wishes to employ a member of his family, particularly his wife. The salary for a wife is not an allowable expense, and that applies also to professional men whose wives may wish to assist in the office. I realize that there may be room for abuse there, but I do not think that that is any reason for the minister not having given consideration to this matter.
The hon. member for York-Simcoe also stressed the need to reduce the number of forms required to be filled and filed by small businesses. I suppose the problem is just as bad for big business, but at least big business has the staff and the expertise needed to fill out these forms in some manner that is less painful to big business than to small business.
If a small businessman cannot complete his forms on his own, he needs to employ professional help, such as lawyers or accountants, to help him in this area. The hon. member for York-Simcoe suggested that small businessmen should be paid a fee for each form they are required to fill out. I think that was a dramatic suggestion that the hon. member made, but I am sure he realizes that that might tend to increase the bureaucracy, and in fact another form would be required to be filled out in order just to get the refund or credit, as he suggested, for filling out forms. But the point needs to be repeated that the hon. member for York-Simcoe was making, that small businessmen need relief from this kind of government intervention in day to day business affairs.
Another area that was touched on in the budget was the write offs for the oil industry. I thought it was interesting that individuals are now to be allowed to write off 100 per cent of their exploration costs. It is interesting to note that the budget was silent on the treatment of development and acquisition costs in the oil industry. I am not sure how useful these provisions would be because in Canada, I suggest, there would be very few individuals who would go into the oil exploration business, which is a very high risk business requiring immense amounts of capital usually not available to individuals. However, there is the possibility of forming syndicates which result in a co-operative effort, and the individuals in the syndicate are treated as individuals for tax purposes.
As I said, the budget was silent on the matter of development and acquisition costs. I was able to get the latest figures available, which were for 1974. We find that in 1974 exploration expenditures were just over $900 million for oil, and development expenditures in that year were $600 million. Both of the figures are admittedly small when compared with the royalties collected from the oil industry in that year which were $1.3 billion, almost equal to the total exploration and development costs. The point is that fully 40 per cent of the total exploration and development expenditures have not been dealt with in this budget, and I feel the minister has done a disservice to the industry and to individuals who might wish to go into a syndicate to explore for oil which Canada and the world needs so badly when he failed to deal with $600 million figure in 1974, which undoubtedly will be larger in the current year.
Today I met some officers of a major Canadian oil company and I find that under the present rules, which
The Budget-Mr. Clarke
were not changed by this budget, it is still better for a Canadian owned oil company to explore in a foreign country. This strange set of circumstances arises because the government has not given sufficient encouragement to Canadian companies to explore in their own country. The combined operation of world oil prices and government involvement by way of taxes and royalties has combined to produce a situation where Canadian oil is less profitable to the Canadian oil company than U.S. oil or oil from some other foreign land.
I was most disappointed with the budget for a number of reasons. I suppose I can summarize them and say it was because the budget in no way deals with the basic problem. I think it was called a stand pat budget, or a few other calm words like that. Certainly it was not much different from last year's budget in regard to the bottom line, so to speak. We have another deficit of some $4.5 billion. The government does not seem to realize-although the hon. member for York-Simcoe explained it very carefully, I thought, and certainly the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) did not agree-that the only way to balance the budget and to change things materially in this country is to cut down government expenditures. The government at the federal level is the only one that can control these things.
There is no way that any other government, any other corporation or business, or any individual could operate as irresponsibly as the federal government itself operates. In the budget the minister even ignored the advice of the Economic Council of Canada which earlier this year in a lengthy report had recommended that one of the solutions for the unemployment insurance dilemma was to create government jobs. There is no suggestion in this budget to create government jobs, and I sense from the feeling of the House that many members will have trouble going along with the proposed regulations on unemployment insurance cut backs, the extended period for qualifying, because of the situation in their areas. Certainly the government should have had a closer look at the creation of government jobs in order to cut down on the abuses, because if a man is offered and refuses a government job which has been created to fill his needs then he has no right to continued benefits.
One of the big expenditures still is the carrying charges on government debt, which I believe amount to $400 million, and yet there is nothing in the budget, and the government apparently continues to refuse to consider, any method that might reduce government investment and therefore reduce the interest charges contained in the budget. If we got rid of a few of these huge government investments we would find the annual deficits reduced on these various government enterprises. I do not want to go into a great deal of detail on these but I would like to mention a few examples. One of them is the hotels which CNR runs for no apparent need.
There are many hoteliers in this country who are able to provide adequate if not luxurious hotel rooms and make a profit at it. Our government requires the CNR to invest the taxpayers' money in hotels and, not only that, they create a loss and a cash drain every single year. I have asked before, and I repeat it now, that the government consider the reduction of investment in such things. I do not restrict

May 27, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Clarke
it to these ventures only; I refer also, for example, to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
