I do not think there is any reason for the government of this country to run a radio system or television system and incur huge losses every year. Those installations are a drain on taxpayers' capital, and interest and operating cost are enormous as well. Someone may well say that we would not have that service if we did not have the government providing it, but it is easy to point to telephone companies all across this country which are not government operated, and with licensing it is a simple matter to ensure that the licence holder provides service in unprofitable areas.
I deplore the investment of taxpayers' dollars in this country in public works. There are huge, huge investments. The Department of Public Works is the largest landlord in the country. There is no evidence to indicate that the department is able to provide space for government departments at anything like a competitive rate because there is not any competition. The stories of waste and inefficiency in that department are legend, and I think some examination of the problem in that enormous area is warranted, but we see none.
The Post Office bears consideration. There is a licensing possibility in the Post Office which is going to need over $1 billion in funds this year, and that is a questionable use of taxpayers' money when there is a huge deficit year after year.
I was interested to read and to compare two statements which I would like to read. One of them was by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). It was made in Ottawa in January of this year at the Canadian Club. The Prime Minister said-
I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but his allotted time has expired. He may continue with unanimous consent. Is there unanimous consent?
Agreed.
No.
The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra.
I had no idea that my time was-

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. When the consent was requested, I shook my head, and I did not wish the hon. gentleman to continue. The hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell) will be seeking the floor in order to contribute to this debate, and I think we should continue in that manner.
Never mind.
Order, please. I would suggest that the parliamentary secretary should say no. I cannot recognize a head shake. Does the hon. member have unanimous consent?
Agreed.

speechtext: No.
Mr. Speaker-

Mr. Speaker, I rise on the point of order raised by the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Blais). I distinctly hear the question, but unfortunately we did not hear the headshake of the parliamentary secretary, and I would question the procedure of putting the question twice when unanimous consent has already been given.
Does the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) have unanimous consent to continue?
Agreed.
No.
Mr. Speaker-
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. This is the Parliament of Canada, not a gathering of Shakers.
Hear, hear!

The only way a contribution can be made in this Chamber is surely by word of mouth and by voice, and I heard nothing at all when Your Honour put the question. With all due respect, the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) received unanimous consent to continue.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened to the debate, and I share the view expressed by the hon. member who has just spoken with respect to the shaking of a head. Moreover, if that was not enough, the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell), being the gentleman he is and who would have been the next speaker on the list, rose and indicated that he was prepared to allow the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) to finish his speech.
Frankly, I do not think Your Honour made a ruling on the second and third occasion. I think, however, that Your Honour did make a ruling when you called upon the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra to finish his speech. That was the ruling you made, and I say that with respect. If that is the case, and if Your Honour agrees with that-and I hope you do, and I hope you agree with the spirit of good fellowship displayed by the hon. member for Scarborough East-I would ask that you allow the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra to finish his remarks.
The Chair does not operate by sign language, and I suggest that the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra continue with his speech.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Go shake your head behind the curtain. What a jerk!

Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
May 27, 1976

Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, there was more than one no, but apart from that I just point out that the reason we are not acceding to the request is the misuse which has been made by the opposition of the privilege to continue. On two separate occasions I have been held up, for half an hour while the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was supposed to be finishing a speech, and again today for twenty minutes while the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau) was finishing his speech. I think the rules should be changed to allow two or three minutes for a member to finish his speech, but not a continuation for another speech on top of the speech already given.
Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the hon. member rising on a point of order?
Yes, I am.
He is infallible.

Do you guys think that's funny? You get paid for it.
Despite the ignorance on the other side, Mr. Speaker, in making reference to a member of this House getting up on a point of order, and making religious overtones, I want to protest strongly that the rules as I have seen them used as a result of gentlemanly courtesy in this House ought to be extended to hon. members when they go overtime for a few minutes, and even though there was an abuse by an hon. member who has served as a prime minister of this country, and so on, that should not be a reason to stop somebody from having a few extra minutes, especially when we consider that Tuesday night we sat here for an hour and a half while outside the whole thing had been given to television and the press before hand, and a big farce was made of this parliament. Let the man go on for a few minutes.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. I am given to understand that unanimous consent was given, and the only member who seemed to have opposed in time was an hon. member who shook his head. Only after the Chair recognized the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) so that he could complete his remarks did somebody stand up and raise the question again.
Rather than hon. members asking the Chair to read the minds of hon. members on both sides of the House, I think it would be very much more simple if we would allow the hon. member to complete his remarks within the next few minutes, and then we can proceed to another hon. member. At the same time I understand that some members might complain about some unanimous consent that they might have given in the past, or even this afternoon. But this is their choice and their responsibility. The Chair should not be put in a position where it has to decide how much reasonable time should be allowed to another member to complete his remarks. If consent is given to allow the hon. member to complete, I am sure the privilege has never been abused, so I think the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra should be allowed to complete his remarks.
The Budget-Mr. O'Connell

Mr. Speaker, I should like to inform hon. members opposite that I would have been finished several minutes ago if I had been given the opportunity. As far as the deputy House leader for the government is concerned, I would simply say that next time he should shake his head a little louder.
I was going to read two short paragraphs which I thought were significant, Mr. Speaker. One was a statement made by the Prime Minister in January this year before the Canadian Club in Ottawa. I should like to compare it with the statement made a few days later in the National Diet in Tokyo by Prime Minister Miki.
The Prime Minister said:
The most pressing reality is inflation. The most urgent national need is for all of us to co-operate in making sure that our anti-inflation program works. An essential part of the program is to search for ways to make the economy work better in the future .. .ways which will prevent a serious recurrence of inflation, promote healthy growth, reduce unemployment, and reduce the need for imposed controls.
In the same month Prime Minister Miki of Japan said:
We are surrounded by many pitfalls, recession, unemployment, and increasing prices. But we must promote economic development without inflation, without stumbling into any of these pitfalls, and we are determined to achieve this goal, without resorting to autocratic economic controls, by liberal and democratic means based on intelligence, forbearance and co-operation, of the government, corporations, labour unions and individual citizens.
I would end my remarks by saying that the problems facing these two great countries are similar. I think it is interesting that the Prime Minister of each stressed cooperation. It is obvious from this budget that the Government of Canada does not intend to seek co-operation in a meaningful way. That is evidenced by the fact that it announced cuts in expenditures, but in fact expenditures are going up by 16 per cent.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to follow the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke). In my remarks I should like to refer to what appear to me to be some of the general questions arising at this time on the matter of economic management and I am going to include, to some extent, social management.
Before getting into that I want to add my words of congratulations to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), and I want to do this, in a broader context than on this budget alone. The budget has, I think, been accepted by the public as pretty finely tuned to the needs in the economy of today. The general acceptance of it and the fact that it has been described by some as a neutral budget is in itself testimony to the broader economic policies set in motion by the minister and the government eight or ten months ago. To the extent, and I believe it is a significant extent, that the minister and the government have their role in managing the economy, the course has been well set, and this budget is not required to alter it in any significant way. I offer my congratulations to the minister on a general economic management role that I think is being carried out very effectively.

Hear, hear!

May 27, 1976
The Budget-Mr. O'Connell

It is at that level that I should like to talk about some economic questions. I want to do it in the shadow, one might say, of the constitutional discussion that is again in front of us.
Some people look upon the shared-cost programs-the DREE type of program where the federal and provincial governments are quite closely interwoven in their economic and social activities-as reflecting intrusions of the federal government into provincial spheres. Other people might say there is so much ambiguity in our constitution that it invites this kind of intrusion and what we need is a constitution that has more clarity in it; that we want to get it back to Canada to change the respective legislative responsibility of the two levels of government; that we want to amend sections 91 and 92 to place the fiscal resources in the hands of those who have certain legislative responsibilities and, perhaps, change the whole level of responsibility. I am one of those who does not believe the latter course is necessary. I think the ambiguity itself of the constitution is one of the benefits of the Canadian Constitutional process for it permits the process in which the political dynamics are more important than the nice legal questions that arise when a constitution is clearly set out. That is a general reflection, Mr. Speaker.
When one discusses these questions in terms of the shared cost programs one finds that today there is the federal desire to put a cap on some of the programs. I am going to use the word capping to refer to the federal and, I suppose, provincial desire to bring some general control to the open-ended character of the shared-cost programs.
The other approach is for the provinces to say, "We want you to transfer tax points to us and let us clarify our jurisdiction; ours is the health jurisdiction; ours is the educational jurisdiction; give us the fiscal resources; let us disentangle ourselves from this rather ambiguous circumstance of shared costs."
We all know too well the arguments about pre-empting provincial priorities for me to try to repeat them here. I want to suggest that the capping process hopefully will succeed in bringing expenditures under control without leading to the disentanglement and the transfer of tax points to the provinces, since it is really the provinces with the greatest incomes where a transfer of tax points, one percentage point, for example, will yield the greatest revenues and that we are likely as the parliament of Canada to lose the capacity to perform the role of the parliament of Canada in inter-regional equities, was through the DREE program, for example, as through other shared-cost programs, and also the role of inter-personal equities through various programs that some would say are more logical in the provincial jurisdiction, such as, for example, family allowances.
I should like to make an argument to the House that capping is the right expenditure policy to follow, that it should not lead the parliament of Canada to agree to the disentanglement approach that some of the stronger provinces are seeking.
If we are to stay with the shared-cost approach, an approach permitted by our constitutional ambiguities, then we owe it to the provinces to make changes and not

maintain a rigid stance. And here I criticize the government stance, as I understand it. It seems to me that if present legislation means that we shall have to put caps on shared-cost programs, we ought to be prepared to consider closely relevant legislation.
In introducing programs we have laid down rigid national standards to which we say the provinces must adhere. That is to say, we have asked the provinces to participate in high cost programs, when lower cost programs which would not be cost shared may have been available to the provinces. We are, in that sense, by passing rigid legislation, forcing on the provinces high cost programs which do not seem appropriate in light of over-all national policy. Instead of putting a cap on such expenditures would it not be better to introduce more flexible programs of the kind I mentioned? Would that not be more advantageous than puting a cap on expenditures?
I think, too, that capping, or tying these expenditures in areas of the national economy to the percentage increase in the gross national product obliges us to respond to provincial overtures for greater provincial participation in or influence on national economic policies. Surely if we have drawn provinces into social programs in fields of health, hospitalization, education and other fields which require high expenditure flows, we should give the provinces some assurance that the economic policies of the government will lead to economic growth and, therefore, that tax yields on provincial resources will be great enough to permit the provinces to meet the growth of their social programs. I say, therefore, that more than capping is required.
We need a closer interweaving of federal and provincial economic and social policies. I would add, and I am thinking in terms of the post-control period which is now being discussed, that there must also be a greater involvement in policy-making of the major elements of the economy, including the labour movement, the industrial sector, and the agricultural sector. Let us in general say that we must adopt a different approach from the one we adopted in the past when we thought too much in terms of the federal-provincial approach and neglected other elements of the economy.
All this is possible because of the ambiguities in our constitution. These areas are not so clearly spelled out that we can say that they are confined within certain jurisdictional boundaries. Our constitution makes possible a planning process under which some programs are centralized in one period, and decentralized in another. It permits a shared approach to problems of national significance and permits the government to play a role in equalizing income as between one region and another.
Our DREE programs are perhaps the clearest model of this process involving a sharing of policy formulation and management. Perhaps such programs will not do as models for other areas of concern, yet we should stop to consider what is taking place under DREE by virtue of the ambiguities in our constitution. One sees the provinces involved in the administration of programs; at the same time policy is developed jointly with the federal government, as is the management of some programs. I trust hon. members will agree that this is not happening because some provinces are fiscally weaker than others and have therefore allowed the federal government to act in areas under their jurisdic-
May 27, 1976

tion because they are weak. Instead we should see in such examples signs that it is possible to undertake, federally and provincially, joint planning in these areas.
I shall now raise what may be a heresy on my side of the House and ask hon. members to consider whether, when they talk about patriating the constitution, they are prepared to bring it back with the addition of a rigid amending procedure which allows various regions of the country a veto. It is possible that unanimous consent would be needed to amend sections 91 and 92. That might make no sense, until we remember that our history and experience show that these things do not matter all that much. Yes, there is in that ambiguity-I use the word again-room for us to come to a consensus through the political process. In that way we can develop programs which meet national concerns and which are sometimes under federal and sometimes under provincial jurisdiction.
Having levied criticisms at the federal government for not seeing this process as a two-way street, and having suggested that we are prepared for the sake of national objectives to participate in DREE programs, and that the provinces by allowing us to participate are allowing us to share in the management, development, and planning of policies which fall under provincial jurisdiction, I now ask are we prepared to let the provinces play a bigger role in over-all economic planning?
That is a very good question.

Can we reach our social objectives by following that route? Perhaps we could respond to the opening the Minister of Finance gave us in his budget speech when he suggested that perhaps we might adopt a new approach to the budgetary process, and approach different from that of the past. I hope and trust that he was talking not only of secrecy in the formulation of the budget but also of greater federal-provincial collaboration, and of collaboration by other elements in the economy which play a necessary role. If there is any reluctance in this regard surely it is a reluctance of the federal government. We must ask ourselves why is this so?
Does the government feel, having followed for the last 40 years the prescriptions of the Keynesian approach to economics, that it cannot devolve the responsibility for fiscal resources to the provinces? Is that the reason? Or has the government felt that so great is its responsibility for managing the economy that it cannot permit the intrusion or intervention of provinces in the development of general national policies? In this regard let me allude to the industrialization of western Canada, and to the kind of policy which might emerge if there were greater provincial input in that particular area.
I now wish to refer to government revenues. Before me I have a table which shows revenues by level of government before and after intergovernmental transfers on a national accounts basis. If we go back 25 years to 1950 we find that the federal government's share, after intergovernmental transfers, was 61 per cent. Today that figure is 40 per cent. Clearly there has been a significant drop in the federal government's share of revenues, from 61 per cent to 40 per cent. In the same 25-year period the provincial share of revenues rose from 22 per cent, in round numbers, to 39 per cent.
The Budget-Mr. O'Connell
Is our reluctance based on the fact that we feel we need all the control that is left at the margin so that the leverage we do have in fiscal and monetary terms does not have to be over-utilized in order to get effects on the national economy to perform a stabilization of growth? I do not think that is a satisfactory argument. However, there may be some validity to it.
It seems that the way out of the dilemma, if there is one, is to involve the provinces and other segments of the economy, as the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) is attempting to do in his tripartite Council to involve them in the process of policy development. I am sure it would be performed in a responsible way so that the provincial fiscal policies would be adjusted to some extent with national policies. The social policies at both levels of government could be in accord with some consensus as to the capabilities of the economy from time to time and the appropriate policies which would enlarge those capabilities, which must be both levels of government. The federal government cannot do it on its own nor can the provinces on their own.
What one sees happening is that over the past 25 years where we have seen a dramatic shift in the control of revenues between the two levels of government, the total spending of the state has risen dramatically. I have here a statistic that is important for the case I am trying to make-total expenditures of all levels of government as a proportion of the gross national product over 25 years. In 1950, 21 per cent of the gross national product was spent by the three levels of government. Today it is 41 per cent. Therefore the state as a whole plays a much larger role in the national economy.
The federal government's leverage in spending has been a reducing share while the others have grown, it might be argued from the point of view of a reluctant federal government to see more provincial participation in policy making. It might be argued that the provinces have so much control over fiscal resources now that they could frustrate national economic policies. They do have that leverage, but what they are asking for is to get into the national policy making where they could play a more responsible role than if we disentangle.
If we say, "Here are some tax points, go your way, this is your jurisdiction". I do not think that would not serve the best interests of the country as a whole because the problems arose in a comprehensive context. They arose in different ways in different regions. Therefore we must be implicated as a national government and they must be implicated because of their jurisdiction.
As I see it, the approach to the post control period lies in the fact that problems are more comprehensive. There is greater uncertainty with regard to policy because of the great degree of change and more interrelatedness between one thing and another.
We can only meet these difficulties by developing an institutional framework for a more interwoven process. We have a constitution that has sufficient ambiguities to permit this. We have experience in such programs as DREE plus the federal contribution to education, medicare, and hospitalization. We have all that background to guide us.
13924

The Budget-Mr. Andre
We have needs that involve both levels. The plea I make to the minister is that he not fall for disentanglement. Do not go that route. Instead, have an institutional structure that will permit capping to be the right process. The price is to make our legislation more flexible so that programs can change. The provinces should be able to choose lower cost programs over the most expensive ones because they happen to be cost shared. That would bring in a process of much greater involvement of all levels of government. In my opinion the problem in the past has resided in a rather reluctant federal process.
I again congratulate the Minister of Finance for opening that corridor, as it were, giving us that opening through saying I would like to look at a different approach. I hope that other members of the House will agree that it lies in federal-provincial action rather than disentanglement.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to begin by congratulating the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell) on his address. I was particularly interested in his latter remarks with regard to increased co-operation in an institutional way between the federal and provincial governments. He has brought to the attention of the minister and the House a very interesting and useful concept.
The past few years have seen the growth of regional difficulties and divisions within this country. This has caused a great deal of concern to a lot of thinking Canadians. I share many of the views of the hon. member for Scarborough East. This arises from the fact that I have considered this particular problem and possible ways of arriving at a solution.
One notion that intrigues me is the possibility of an institutionalization of the federal-provincial conference in a manner that might work toward accomplishing the sorts of goals the hon. member has brought to the attention of the House. I notice the minister paid attention to that address. I hope that tonight has seen the germination of an idea that will grow, bringing with it political institutions in this country that will better serve the needs of Canadians.
I am sure this is a first for me. After congratulating one member opposite, I move to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) on one part of his budget. In particular I am referring to the amendments to the Income Tax Act as they apply to individual taxpayers investing in the oil and gas industry. This is in reference to the principal business test.
It may be of value to outline a bit of the history of this particular aspect of the Income Tax Act and the effect it has had on this country. There is a lesson there that we would do well to learn in order to prevent similar mistakes in the future. The Income Tax Act rightfully provides that when filing an income tax return and paying income tax, one must consolidate one's income. Otherwise someone who makes, say, two incomes of $5,000 from two separate sources and files two separate returns would pay less than the man who made $10,000 from one source of income, which would be unfair. That applied almost universally as a principle thoughout the Income Tax Act with one solitary exception, and that had to do with the oil and gas industry.

In the oil and gas industry, if one formed a company and drilled an oil well and the hole turned out to be dry, that was an expense which could be deducted from one's income if one were in the oil industry. But if one were not in the oil industry as a principal business one could not deduct that expense from business income. This meant that fresh capital for the industry had to come from outside sources. In this respect Canadian law was unique, at least as far as developed countries were concerned. It had no equivalent in the United States or in Europe. The result was that Americans came to drill wells in Canada. Doctors, lawyers, those with discretionary income could use pretaxed dollars for this purpose, but Canadians could not.
This aspect of Canadian law more than any other single aspect is responsible for the oil and gas industry presently being 90 to 95 per cent foreign owned. It has been a source of grievance on the part of the oil industry for as far back as anybody can remember. It has been a grievance felt by the people of Alberta as far back as anyone can remember. Delegation after delegation came to Ottawa to seek amendment to this law. There are scores of examples of geologists coming up with what is called, in the terms of the trade, a "good play", seeking people willing to invest, but finding it difficult to interest Canadians, or, to put it in a more positive way, finding it easier to attract Americans to invest, with the result that a number of American millionaires were created-American owners of Canadian oil and gas businesses. This situation has been with us these last 25 years and, as I have said, it is the single most important reason for our oil and gas being largely foreign owned.
Finally, in the budget last Tuesday the minister removed that restrictive provision, and for doing so he deserves the thanks of all Canadians because it is a move which is long, long overdue. It is a temporary provision as matters stand but I am certain that after three years of examination the finance minister, whoever he may be, will realize that this was a positive step and will make it a permanent part of our taxation system.
My hon. friend from Vancouver Quadra raised the question of the application of development and acquisition expenses in regard to the principal business'test. This is an area which warrants examination and I am hopeful the minister will look into that aspect of the provision and see fit to improve it so as to place Canadians on an equal footing with nationals of other countries when it comes to investing in their own industry. This makes such good common sense that I am at a loss to understand why it took so long for the government to come around to that point of view. I notice that the minister has departed and perhaps that is appropriate since I have just voiced the last compliment I intend to pay him, maybe for a long time. There are other features of the budget which are far less laudable.
One most important omission as far as I am concerned is the lack of any measures addressed to Canada's outstanding trade deficit. "Outstanding" is almost too mild an adjective to apply to our trade deficit in manufacturing, in high technology, because in 1975, the last year for which figures are available, it amounted to $8,400 million, an astronomical figure. Had it occurred in any other country in the western world it would have shaken the govern-
May 27, 1976

ment; it might even have brought it down. Think of what that represents in jobs. Think of what it represents in terms of the capacity of our economy. That sort of trade imbalance is what caused the government of Britain to bring in the draconian measures to which Britons have been subjected, measures which have included devaluation and currency controls, as well as other forms of control.
The mere existence of this horrendous trade imbalance has caused a considerable number of Canadians, more than just a few, to examine their personal portfolios-I am speaking now of those Canadians who have a few dollars invested-from the point of view of transferring their assets abroad before the government is forced to impose currency control to prevent such transfers. This feeling is abroad in Canada based on the figures which have been published, and it is startling to find that the government has failed to address itself to this problem with positive measures intended to reverse a disastrous trend. The figure I gave was for 1975 but it reflects a five or six year trend which is devastating in its implications. Mr. Speaker, may I call it ten o'clock?
A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 40 deemed to have been moved.

subtopic: MANPOWER-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO FIND EMPLOYMENT FOR STUDENTS
MANPOWER-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO FIND EMPLOYMENT FOR STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, two nights ago the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) brought down his budget. It was at best what the economists call a neutral budget. It was neutral in the sense that the minister saw no reason to cut taxes in order to give Canadians more purchasing power or to indicate any intention on the part of the government to begin a program of public works which could create jobs in large numbers.
It was, to say the least, a surprising budget in view of the fact that unemployment for the month of April, the last month for which we have figures, stood at a 15-year high. The national employment rate jumped sharply to 7.4 per cent of the work force during April. According to Statistics Canada, 769,000 people were out of work, the highest number of unemployed and the highest rate, seasonally adjusted, which Canada has seen since the year 1961.
The only two provinces in which the unemployment rate did not rise in April over the month before were New Brunswick and Manitoba. In British Columbia the rate rose to 9.7 per cent. In Ontario it rose to 6.2 per cent, and in Quebec to 8.3 per cent. In Nova Scotia the rate increased to 9.1 per cent. Newfoundland had the dubious honour of having the highest rate of 14 per cent. That unemployment
Adjournment Debate
rate is particularly serious for the young people, the students.
According to studies completed by the Department of Manpower, last year the unemployment rate among students was 10 Vi per cent. That was at a time when the unemployment rate for all Canadians was much lower than it is now or will be this summer. Last year close to I'A million young people, students, were looking for jobs at some time during the summer; 10 Vi per cent of them were unemployed during the summer at a time when the Government of Canada had established programs which provided well over 50,000 jobs for students who were looking for work.
This year we have seen the end of the Opportunities for Youth Program and the LIP Program. We have also seen the end of most of the programs which the Government of Canada operated in other years. This year the government proposes to hire not more than 12,000 students, a decrease of more than 30,000.
The minister's answer to my plea was that the government is working with private employers and is encouraging them to hire more students than they hired in other years. I am sure the government will try. I am sure the public servants will work at that, but at a time when unemployment is at the highest rate at which it has been for 15 years employers will not be in a position to give much help in this way. It is obvious to me this is one more instance of government bungling.
The concern of the government about inflation is so great that no attention is being paid to the serious problem of unemployment. The Globe and Mail reported a few days ago that the Department of Manpower and Immigration had in fact realized the gravity of the situation and had worked out very detailed and complete plans for job creation programs, programs which would employ somewhere between 100,000 and 200,000 of the people now unemployed. Of course such programs would be expensive. The department has estimated that such programs would cost $1 billion.
I do not suggest for one moment that $1 billion is a small amount of money. However, we must realize that the Government of Canada last year had to subsidize the unemployment insurance fund to meet the claims of those people who were unemployed and eligible to draw unemployment insurance by an amount of $lVi billion. This is money that was collected in the form of taxes, to be paid to people who were not working. That seems to me to be a form of insanity. Surely it would be far better that people who want to work and are able to work should be working at productive jobs. There are many things which need to be done in Canada, there are people to do the work, and there are projects which need doing.
I urge the government to stop focusing its attention on the problem of inflation and to begin to pay attention to the very serious problem of the unemployed, particularly of the unemployed students who need jobs this summer if they are to go back to their studies this fall.

the private sector to hire students during the summer, as temporary employees.

subtopic: AIR CANADA-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION OF FINANCE BRANCH AT WINNIPEG BY AUDITOR GENERAL
AIR CANADA-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION OF FINANCE BRANCH AT WINNIPEG BY AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over the last couple of weeks I have been requesting an investigation into the Air Canada finance branch in Winnipeg and an assurance that the finance branch will not be moved to Montreal. I have received some rather ridiculous answers from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang). The Prime Minister stated that the government should not run one of its Crown corporations from the floor of the House of Commons. I certainly agree with that. If Air Canada appeared before the Standing Committee on Transport and

Communications on a regular basis, then we most certainly would not have to discuss this Air Canada operation on the floor of the House. But Air Canada has not been before the standing committee since the last parliament, in 1973, and thus this is a lot of utter nonsense.
I would also like to point out that we recently spent almost $400,000 doing an Air Canada inquiry report on the operations of Air Canada, and all through the whole document the problems within the finance branch in Winnipeg and problems of communications right through the whole Air Canada operation are pointed out. All we can assume is that this has been dumped into the garbage and that the only thing which has been done is that the former Air Canada president has resigned and we have a new president. I certainly hope we get an explanation from the parliamentary secretary tonight as to why this $400,000 study has been completely ignored by the government. I see that there is a smirk on the face of the parliamentary secretary. Obviously he is picking this up from his minister, who is always quite jovial about the matter.
Yesterday we found out that the president of Air Canada, Mr. Taylor, said that he is going to be applying for an air fare increase. There is an absolute catastrophe in the Air Canada finance branch in Winnipeg, a complete breakdown in the auditing system, a loss of millions of dollars, and he has the utter audacity to say he is going to ask for a fare increase. I have taken some steps myself because I do not expect the government to do a damned thing about it. I have written to Mr. Benson, the head of CTC, and requested that he not allow any more fare increases. I asked him to review the last one. Obviously the CTC was not aware of the financial fiasco and the financial mess in Air Canada, and had he known, perhaps Mr. Benson would not have allowed the last increase, which took place on April 18.
I have received much information from CALEA members with regard to the financial breakdown, and it would appear that they are more concerned about Air Canada's financial problems and its operation than the government and Air Canada management are. I would just like to point out some of the problems they are experiencing. Here is an example. This is a document which came out of the Air Canada office at Heath Row, London, England. That office points out the following:
Several times a year we have been traced and on one occasion threatened with legal action by our Grosvenor Hill landlord lor non-receipt of quarterly rental payment (14,000 pounds). Last year the manager, disbursements, was provided with copies of twenty representative letters from suppliers all relating to their need to have invoices paid within ten days or 'cash on delivery'. Cash flow is a very real problem in the U.K. firms today.
The information that office received from the Winnipeg finance office was as follows:
I understand from the accounts office supervisor that we cannot expect any positive action for the next 12-18 months as he has been informed that the delay is due to a backlog of programming time in the C & SS branch in Winnipeg.
What an embarrassment to an Air Canada office overseas. They cannot pay their bills and, as I pointed out about six weeks ago, this Air Canada office was threatened with having its gas and light cut off because the finance

branch in Winnipeg could not get money over there to pay the bills. This is a lot of nonsense.
In addition, billings to Air Canada from other airlines do not receive a complete audit. Items billed for $75 or less are assumed to be correct and paid without question.
Air Canada's own internal auditors endeavoured to audit the refund bank drafts account in 1975. This account is not less than $2.5 million per month, about $30 million per year. They finally gave up, and that account remains unaudited since 1972. Therefore over the past four years a $120 million account has been in question. When I bring matters like this up, what do I get? I get a snickering grin from the Minister of Transport and he says that he trusts Air Canada to do a great job. Well, I do not think it is doing a great job. I also wrote a letter to the Auditor General asking him to get his staff in there and to get this ungodly mess straightened out.
In the CALEA members' bulletin dated September 12 they mentioned that there was at that time a backlog of
250,000	unreported Air Canada tickets in the ticket inventory and control section of the revenue accounting department. Those are tickets sold by Air Canada sales offices, travel agents, commercial accounts, etc. Those are the very reasons why Mr. Taylor should be before the standing committee, so that we can ask him and get this mess straightened up rather than putting out news releases to tell us that he needs a fare increase.
This is one of the highlights of the reports from CALEA. When we hear corporate management talk about a $90 million loss in revenue this year, and when we see load factors reported that refuse to accommodate such a large loss, it takes little intelligence to determine that something is wrong.
It has been much belaboured by the media that Air Canada has an antiquated "Mickey Mouse" accounting procedure-

Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to dwell at any length on the hon. member's rude, insulting, and thoroughly ill-founded allegations with respect to the status of the Estey report or the other items which are on the agenda of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications. Adjournment Debate
A simple clerical error on the part of Warnock Hersey resulted in ticket sales reports not being forwarded for a period of several months, but when this error was discovered the matter was rectified and any outstanding amount paid immediately.
During the past few months Air Canada's finance branch in Winnipeg, has been subjected to a series of disruptive actions by its clerical workers, who are members of the Canadian Airline Employees Association. subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-CONSIDERATIONS ENTERING INTO SALE OF MILITARY EQUIPMENT
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-CONSIDERATIONS ENTERING INTO SALE OF MILITARY EQUIPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 3, 1975, I asked the then acting Prime Minister for information on Canada's sales of military equipment. This was but one of many efforts through oral and written questions to learn the facts of this country's extensive dealing in arms.
After being on the order paper for over a year, a question of mine elicited the reply that we sold arms to 73 countries, ranging from A to Z-Abu Dhabi to Zambia. Taiwan bought arms as recently as 1974.
While the minister declared that we did not sell arms of any kind to countries in the Middle East, I found the list included Iran, Israel, Kuwait, Muscat and Oman, Saudi Arabia, Union of Arab Emirates, countries either in or very interested in the Middle East.
In reference to the Middle East one notes in the reply at page 9367 of Hansard for November 24, 1975, that Israel appears on the list for every year from 1963-1974 while the few Arab states noted are much less frequently on the market. One is struck by the fact that none of the so-called confrontation states, Egypt, Jordan or Syria, are shown as having been sold any Canadian military equipment.
In such a sensitive area and in regard to a situation of such delicacy, this seeming discrimination may be serious indeed. This is especially the case in light of the minister's

Adjournment Debate
denial that the government viewed sales of conventional arms as purely business transactions where the dollar value was the only value worth considering. Indeed the ministerial disquisition on arms sales was one of the most fascinating if totally mystifying verbal exercises I have heard in my 19 years in this Chamber. Some of the gems were, "We do have regard to sales of military equipment of all kinds in all directions"; and again: "We also have some categories that might be termed military equipment of a rather innocent character..." The minister also declaimed, "There are certain types of arms and equipment for warlike purposes that we do not supply. Many of the things we supply are not intended for the purpose of killing people." So moved was he that the sedate and normally restrained member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees), could not forbear the comment, "They are 'soft arms' are they?"
But while the response may have had its hilarious aspect, the subject matter is far from amusing. In absolute terms Canada ranks sixth among the world's arms salesmen, exceeded only by the U.S., the U.S.S.R., France, the U.K., and Italy. Among the merchants of death our peace-loving country is by no means in the background. Although Canadians are often accused of lacking aggressiveness in seeking world markets, we are not such shrinking violets when it comes to peddling death-dealing weaponry or related implements of military conflict.
It is very difficult to get a clear picture of what exactly is our role in the field of arms sales. We are told that much must remain secret lest the breach in confidentiality injure the competitiveness of certain Canadian firms. Because of changing formats and departmental reorganization it is not easy to obtain data on the full role of government in the process. The annual report of the Canadian Commercial Corporation is about as quantitatively informative as the average container of breakfast cereal. To those hon. members desirous of information on this very serious matter I would commend the book "Making a Killing" by Ernie Regehr, and the article in Saturday Night, volume 86, 1971, "Dealing Out Death Discreetly; The Traffic in Canadian Arms", by William Cobban.
I believe we must be more realistic and more revealing on this question. I do not think we can on this or any other question have it both ways. We cannot trot out our selfrighteous purity in the nuclear field and then sell arms of another kind to anyone who wishes to buy them, whether they be in the Third World or elsewhere. If we are to adopt the attitude that business is business and who kills whom with Canadian arms is not an issue, then let us say so. But to suggest seriously that Canada sells only gentle, kindly items of military hardware is a bit much even in this age of double talk and slick salesmanship. If our considerations are based on moral judgments and values it does not matter whether we are talking about the nuclear destruction of 100,000 people or the killing of a few hundred so-called political enemies by rifles or machine guns which were in their heyday in the second world war.
In my school days I recall a poem which reflected upon the then sophisticated armaments of the so-called civilized west and their destruction of the peoples of other areas. The author described these machines of mass killing as,
"means of death, and so may be a dagger in a damsel's hand."
I hope we will have an end to the notion that Canada sells not hard but soft, not bad but good military arms. I hope, Sir, that we will have the whole matter examined, and check out the relationship of principles to pocket books.

speakeroldname: Miss Monique Begin (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-CONSIDERATIONS ENTERING INTO SALE OF MILITARY EQUIPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this subject is of great concern to all Canadians, and quoting Saturday Night, with all due respect to the magazine, is making a farce of providing proper information on this most important and serious matter of arms sales.
I suggest that the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) cannot be serious when he suggests that arms are necessarily for killing. He quoted the House leader who answered in the absence of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) and who, in all good faith, gave as many details as he could. The mixing of answers made to the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) and taking them out of context is, in my opinion, tantamount to intellectual dishonesty.
It is obvious to anyone who takes five minutes to think about it that there are commercial sales of equipment that are not military in nature, not specifically designed for military purposes or that do not have a military function. For example, there is the laser, not to mention almost the complete electronic industry.
I find the rhetoric of the hon. member for Hillsborough nothing more than words; very moving in the way he presents them but absolutely empty. What is worse, they are misleading the Canadian public. It would have been more helpful if he had asked questions about the statistical categories under which fall the so-called sales of arms to foreign countries.
It is important to note that we should distinguish three categories of arms. The first is weapons and ammunition; then military support equipment; and then commercial equipment which may have a military application. I underlined what this might be. The joke of the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees) was really not appropriate in the debate on December 3, 1975.
In general terms our policy is based on the principle that weapons and ammunition and military support equipment will not be supplied to countries considered as representing a possible military threat to Canada; to countries involved in hostilities; to countries where there is an imminent threat of hostilities; to those countries to which U.N. resolutions forbid the export of such equipment, or to regimes pursuing policies contrary to Canadian standards and practices.
I will finish with one additional piece of information, although we should be discussing this question at length. The fact of a sale to an individual country may indicate either that the product sold was military in nature or that the end user would be the military in that country even though the equipment itself was of a purely commercial nature. Some of the countries mentioned by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson) fall into that category.
